title: Understanding and analyzing social and behavioral data
text:
Preface
This book is an introduction to the analysis of social and behavioral data using R. It is designed for complete beginners. No prior programming experience is assumed.
The book is organized into sections, each containing several chapters. You can read the chapters in order, or jump to a specific topic using the table of contents on the left.

title: Understanding and analyzing social and behavioral data
Understanding and analyzing social and behavioral data
Understanding and analyzing social and behavioral data
text:
Section 1: Getting Started Properly
Section 1 lays out the foundations: what R is, how to install it, what the different file types are, and how to perform basic operations. By the end of Section 1 you will have a solid mental model of the R ecosystem and you will be ready to start working with real data.
Additional sections will be added as the book grows.

title: 1  What is R, and why use it?
text:
1.1 What R is
R is a programming language designed for statistics and data analysis. It is also the name of the program that runs the language: when you “use R,” you are typically running a program called R that reads instructions written in the R language and carries them out. In the next chapter we will look more carefully at the difference between the language and the program, since this distinction matters when you install things and when you read documentation.
R is free and open source. Anyone can download it, and the source code is publicly available. It is maintained by a non-profit organization (the R Foundation) and developed by a large international community. Two practical consequences follow. First, your access to R does not depend on an institutional license: you can install it on any computer you have access to, including any computer you own after you leave university. Second, if a particular feature does not exist, anyone can write it, share it, and others can verify what it does. We will return to this idea in Chapter 6 when we discuss packages.
R was created by statisticians, for statistics. Most general-purpose programming languages (Python, Java, JavaScript) treat statistical analysis as one application among many. R treats it as the central use case. The everyday operations of empirical research (fitting a regression, running an ANOVA, computing a correlation matrix, reshaping a dataset for repeated-measures analysis) are part of the language’s basic vocabulary.
crumbs: 1  What is R, and why use it?

title: 1  What is R, and why use it?
section: 1.2 Why use R rather than software like SPSS or Excel?
text:
1.2 Why use R rather than software like SPSS or Excel?
If you have used SPSS, Excel, or similar tools, you know that most of your work happens by clicking. You select a variable, click a menu, choose a test, click “OK.” This is convenient for one-off questions, but it has three costs that grow as your work becomes more serious.
The first cost is reproducibility. When you click through a menu, the actions you took are not automatically recorded in a way that someone else (or you, six months later) can retrace. If a colleague asks “exactly how did you compute this number?”, you have to remember. With R, the answer is in the script: every step of the analysis is written down, and anyone with the script and the data can run it and obtain the same result. This is increasingly required by journals, funders, and pre-registration platforms.
The second cost is detection of errors. When you copy a column of values in Excel and paste it into a new column, the operation is invisible after the fact. You can inspect the final state of the spreadsheet, but you cannot inspect the chain of operations that produced it. When something looks wrong, you often cannot tell where the error was introduced. With R, every step is a line of code. If a result is wrong, you can read the code line by line and find the mistake.
The third cost is scale. Suppose you discover that 30 of your variables need the same correction. In SPSS or Excel, you have to perform the correction 30 times, once per variable. In R, you write the correction once and apply it to all 30 variables in a single line. We will see a concrete example of this in Chapter 6. This is not a small convenience: it can change which research questions are practical to ask.
R has limitations as well, which it is honest to acknowledge. The learning curve at the start is steeper than for SPSS; you cannot simply open a file and click “run analysis.” Error messages can be cryptic when you are starting out. And because the language is large and the package ecosystem is even larger, you are constantly making choices about which tool to use for a given task. This book is designed to guide you through that environment with a small, well-chosen set of tools.
crumbs: 1  What is R, and why use it?

title: 1  What is R, and why use it?
text:
1.3 Instead, if you use R…
R code is a written record of operations on data. A common first impression is that this looks like making things complicated for no reason: extra typing for no obvious benefit. The benefit shows up in three places.
The first place is transparency. A script is a complete description of the analysis. A reviewer, a collaborator, or your future self can read the script and know what you did. Nothing is hidden inside someone’s recollection of a sequence of clicks.
The second place is correction. With code, the whole analysis is visible in front of you, and you can read it from top to bottom to locate exactly where an error was introduced. In a click-based workflow in SPSS or Excel, the sequence of actions you performed is not recorded as a readable trace; if a result looks wrong, you have to “reverse engineer” what you did from memory or from the final state of the data, which is slow and often inconclusive. Once an error is located and fixed in code, you re-run the script and every downstream step updates automatically.
The third place is reuse. The script you write to clean Survey 1 is largely the same script you will use to clean Survey 2. With each project, your toolkit grows, and tasks that took a week the first time take an hour the third time.
For a researcher working with social and behavioral data, the cumulative effect of these three benefits is substantial. The transition is also possible: thousands of researchers have made it, including people with no prior programming background.
crumbs: 1  What is R, and why use it?

title: 1  What is R, and why use it?
text:
1.4 R is “object-based”
You will sometimes hear R described as an “object-oriented” language. The phrase has a specific meaning in computer science (it refers to a design pattern involving classes, methods, and inheritance), and R does support that pattern. But for the way you will use R as a beginner, that strict definition is not the most useful one. We will use a simpler phrase: object-based.
In R, every piece of information you work with is stored as an object. An object is a piece of data that has been given a name. The number 7 stored under the name participants is an object. A whole survey dataset stored under the name data2024 is an object. A correlation matrix stored under the name correlations is also an object.
When you write R code, you spend most of your time doing two things: creating objects, and feeding objects into operations to produce new objects. Here is a small example. Suppose scores is an object containing the test scores of 100 participants. To get the average, you write:

mean(scores)

Here, mean is itself a piece of R, called a function. You feed it the object scores, and it produces a new value: the average. If you want to keep that average around for later, you assign it to a name:

average_score <- mean(scores)

Now average_score is its own object. You can use it elsewhere, just like you used scores.
A few practical implications of this object-based way of working are worth flagging now, even though we will explore them in detail later.
The first implication is that names matter. A well-chosen object name tells you what the object contains. data2024_clean is more useful than df3.
The second implication is that the order of operations is explicit. Each line of code typically takes objects as input and produces objects as output. To understand what a script does, you can read it from top to bottom and watch how objects appear and transform.
The third implication is that the workspace is a collection of named objects. At any given moment, R holds in memory a list of every object you have created. This list is called the environment. We will return to the environment in Chapter 3 and Chapter 4.
You do not need to memorize any of this yet. Notice the vocabulary (object, function, environment), and we will revisit each term with concrete examples in later chapters.
crumbs: 1  What is R, and why use it?

title: 1  What is R, and why use it?
section: 1.5 What this book will and will not teach you
text:
1.5 What this book will and will not teach you
This book is about understanding and analyzing social and behavioral data. The first section focuses on R itself: what it is, how to install it, how the pieces fit together, and how the basic operations work. We are not analyzing real data yet. That comes in later sections.
The reason for this ordering is practical. The most common cause of frustration among new R users is not a particular statistical operation. It is confusion about how R, RStudio, scripts, projects, and the environment relate to each other. When that confusion is cleared up, learning specific analyses becomes a matter of looking up the right function, which is a much smaller problem.
By the end of Section 1, you will be able to install R and RStudio, create and save the relevant kinds of files, perform basic operations, and use existing packages. You will also have a clear mental model that you can use to learn anything else about R, whether or not it is covered in this book.
crumbs: 1  What is R, and why use it?

title: 1  What is R, and why use it?
text:
1.6 Check your understanding
1. Which of the following best describes what R is?

 R is a paid statistical software package developed by IBM. R is a free, open-source programming language designed for statistics and data analysis. R is a graphical user interface that lets you perform statistical tests by clicking through menus. R is a cloud-based application that runs only inside a web browser.

2. Which of the following best summarizes the advantages of R over click-based software for serious research work?

 Reproducibility, error detection, and scaling operations to many variables. Faster computation than SPSS for every analysis. Built-in graphical menus for every common statistical test. Automatic generation of APA-formatted reports without any code.

3. In R, what is an “object”?

 Anything that has been clicked on at least once during the session. A type of file used to save analyses to disk. A piece of information stored under a name, such as a number, a vector, or a dataset. A function that has been written by the R Foundation.

4. Why does coding an analysis (rather than clicking through menus) help with reproducibility?

 Because R automatically records every menu click in a hidden log file. Because R cannot save its work in any other way. Because the script is a complete written record of every step of the analysis, which can be re-run, inspected, and shared. Because R rejects analyses that have not been pre-registered.

5. In the line average_score <- mean(scores), what is mean?

 A function takes one or more objects as input and returns a new object as output. A function is a saved menu setting in R. A function is a way of giving a name to a single number. A function is a type of file extension used by R.

6. In this book, what does it mean to say that R is “object-based”?

 It means that R is the only language with named variables. It means that the information you work with is stored under names, and you create new objects by feeding existing objects into operations. It means that R can only be used to analyze datasets that have been organized into objects beforehand by SPSS. It means that R requires you to define classes and inheritance hierarchies before doing any analysis.
crumbs: 1  What is R, and why use it?

title: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate
text:
2.1 Two pieces of software, one workflow
A common point of confusion for new users is the difference between R and RStudio. They are two separate programs, made by two different organizations, that work together. To use R productively, you will install both, and you will use them at the same time.
The simplest way to picture the relationship is the following. R is the engine. It is the piece of software that actually understands the R language and performs the computations: when you ask for a mean, R is what calculates it. RStudio is the dashboard. It does not perform any statistics on its own. What it provides is a comfortable working environment around R: a place to write scripts, a console where you can type commands, a panel showing the objects you have created, a panel for plots, a file browser, and many other conveniences.
If you install RStudio without installing R first, RStudio will open but it will have nothing to talk to: clicking “Run” will produce an error. If you install R without installing RStudio, R will work, but you will be using a fairly bare interface that most users find harder to navigate. The standard practice is to install both.
This division of labor has a useful consequence: you can update one without the other. The R Foundation releases new versions of R from time to time, and Posit (the company that maintains RStudio) releases new versions of RStudio on a separate schedule. Each can evolve at its own pace.
crumbs: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate

title: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate
text:
2.2 Are there alternatives to RStudio?
Yes. RStudio is the most widely used environment for R, but it is not the only one. Several alternatives exist:

Positron, also developed by Posit, is a newer environment that supports R and Python in a single interface. It is built on the same foundations as Visual Studio Code.
Visual Studio Code (VS Code) with the official R extension provides an R working environment inside a popular general-purpose editor.
Jupyter notebooks with an R kernel provide a notebook-style interface, more common in the Python world but also usable for R.
The plain R console that ships with R itself can be used directly, without any additional environment.

For this book we will use RStudio. The reasoning is practical: it is the environment with the most accessible learning materials, the most stable behavior, and the smoothest integration with the kinds of files (R scripts, R Markdown, R projects) that we will introduce in Chapter 3. If you later want to try one of the alternatives, the underlying R code you write will work in any of them.
crumbs: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate

title: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate
text:
2.3 Installing R
R is distributed by the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN), a network of servers maintained by the R community. You can download R from any of these servers; in practice it is easiest to use the official entry point.
Step by step:

Open a web browser and go to https://cran.r-project.org.
On the home page, find the section “Download and Install R” at the top. There are three links: one for Linux, one for macOS, and one for Windows. Click the link that matches your operating system.
If you are on Windows: click the link that reads “install R for the first time,” then click the large download link at the top of the next page (it will read something like “Download R-X.Y.Z for Windows,” where X.Y.Z is the current version number). The file is a .exe installer. Double-click it and accept the default options at every step. You do not need to change any settings.
If you are on macOS: on the macOS download page, choose the .pkg file that matches your processor. Apple computers built since 2020 use Apple Silicon (M1, M2, M3, M4); older Apple computers use Intel processors. If you are unsure, click the Apple menu in the top-left corner of your screen, choose “About This Mac,” and look at the “Chip” or “Processor” line. Download the matching .pkg file, double-click it, and accept the default options.
If you are on Linux: follow the instructions for your distribution. They differ between Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, and others. Linux users typically have the necessary technical background; if you do not, the simplest approach is to use an Ubuntu-based distribution and follow the Ubuntu instructions on CRAN.

After installation finishes, R is on your computer. You will not normally open it directly; you will reach it through RStudio, which we install next.
crumbs: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate

title: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate
text:
2.4 Installing RStudio
RStudio is distributed by Posit. The free version, called RStudio Desktop (Open Source Edition), is the one most users want. It has all the features you need for the work in this book.
Step by step:

Go to https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/.
The page shows two steps: “Install R” (which you have already done) and “Install RStudio.” Scroll to the second step.
The page typically detects your operating system and offers a single download button. Click it.
If you are on Windows: the file is an .exe installer. Double-click it and accept the default options.
If you are on macOS: the file is a .dmg disk image. Double-click it to open, then drag the RStudio icon into the Applications folder.
If you are on Linux: follow the Linux instructions on the same page. RStudio is provided as a .deb or .rpm package depending on your distribution.

If you are using a university computer where you cannot install software, ask your IT department to install both R and RStudio, or use the cloud version of RStudio at https://posit.cloud, which runs in a browser and requires no installation.

You may find the following short videos helpful as a complement to the written instructions above. They are not the most recent, and the download pages may have changed slightly in appearance, but the essentials of the installation process have not changed.

title: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate
section: 2.5 What you see when you open RStudio for the first time
text:
2.5 What you see when you open RStudio for the first time
Open RStudio. You should see a window divided into three panels (later it will become four, once you create a script). The exact arrangement varies, but the typical default is:

A large panel on the left called the Console. This is where R receives commands and prints results. If you type 2 + 2 and press Enter here, R will print 4.
A panel on the upper right containing several tabs. The most important tab is Environment. This panel will eventually list every object you have created, with its name and a brief description of its contents. When RStudio first opens it is empty.
A panel on the lower right, also with tabs. The most important ones are Files (a built-in file browser), Plots (where graphs you produce will appear), Packages (a list of installed packages, which we will discuss in Chapter 6), and Help (the R documentation system).

You can verify that R and RStudio are talking to each other. Click in the Console, type the following exactly, and press Enter:

2 + 2

R should print [1] 4 on the next line. The [1] is a labeling convention used by R to mark the position of values in long output; for a single value you can ignore it. If you see [1] 4, your installation is working.
Two more checks worth doing the first time:

sessionInfo()

This prints information about your R version, your operating system, and the packages currently loaded. The first line of the output starts with “R version” followed by the version number; this confirms which version of R you are running.

RStudio.Version()

This works only inside RStudio (not in the bare R console) and prints the RStudio version. If both commands work, you have a complete and matched installation.
crumbs: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate

title: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate
text:
2.6 A note on updates
Both R and RStudio release new versions periodically. Updating R requires running the installer again; updating RStudio also requires running its installer again. There is no automatic update process built into either program. For the work in this book, any version of R from 4.2 onwards and any RStudio version from 2023 onwards will work. If you have a working installation, do not feel obliged to update it for now.
crumbs: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate

title: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate
text:
2.7 Check your understanding
1. Which of the following best describes the relationship between R and RStudio?

 R is the dashboard you click on, and RStudio is the engine that performs computations. R and RStudio are two names for the same program. R is the engine that performs computations, and RStudio is a dashboard that provides a comfortable working environment around R. RStudio includes its own version of R and replaces the need to install R separately.

2. Which piece of software actually performs the statistical computations?

 RStudio. R. Microsoft Excel. The web browser used to download the installer.

3. What happens if you install RStudio without first installing R?

 RStudio works without R, because RStudio comes with its own statistical engine built in. RStudio refuses to start. RStudio opens, but it has no engine to talk to, so commands cannot be executed. R is automatically downloaded by RStudio the first time it is launched.

4. Where does R itself come from when you install it?

 CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network. The Apple App Store and the Microsoft Store. GitHub. The RStudio website.

5. Is installing RStudio required to use R?

 It is mandatory: R cannot be used without RStudio. It is discouraged: most experienced users avoid RStudio in favor of the bare console. It is the standard practice for most users, although other environments such as Positron, VS Code, and Jupyter also exist. It is only useful for users on Windows; macOS users should not install it.

6. Which RStudio panel will list the objects you have created during a session?

 The Help panel. The Plots panel. The Environment panel. The Files panel.
crumbs: 2  R, RStudio, and how they relate

title: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown
text:
3.1 Why this chapter exists
When you start using R, you will encounter several different “things” that all live on your computer and that all seem related to R: scripts, RData files, R projects, the environment, R Markdown files. New users frequently confuse these. The confusion is not unfounded; the names are similar, the file extensions are similar, and the documentation often assumes you already know which is which.
This chapter introduces each of them and clarifies what they are for. By the end, you should be able to answer the question “what kind of file should I create to do this?” for each of the situations you will encounter.
A useful preliminary distinction: some of these things are files saved on your computer, while one of them (the environment) is a state held in memory while R is running. We will start with the in-memory thing because it underpins everything else.
crumbs: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown

title: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown
section: 3.2 The environment: what R is holding right now
text:
3.2 The environment: what R is holding right now
When you run R (typically through RStudio), R holds in memory a list of all the objects you have created during the current session. This list is called the environment, or sometimes the workspace.
For example, suppose you open RStudio, type the following in the Console, and press Enter after each line:

participants <- 100
mean_age <- 21.4
condition_labels <- c("control", "treatment")

You have now created three objects: participants, mean_age, and condition_labels. They are all in the environment. The Environment panel in RStudio (upper right) will show them: their names, their types, and a short preview of their contents.
The environment is not a file. It exists only while R is running. When you close R, the environment is gone. If you reopen R later and want those objects back, you have to either re-create them by running the same code, or load them from a saved file.
This brings us to the next distinction.
crumbs: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown

title: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown
text:
3.3 The R script (.R file)
An R script is a plain-text file with the extension .R. It contains R code: the same code you would type into the Console, but saved in a file so you can re-run it later.
To create a script in RStudio: in the menu, click File > New File > R Script. A blank document opens in a new panel (typically the upper-left). You can type code there.

participants <- 100
mean_age <- 21.4
condition_labels <- c("control", "treatment")

To save the script, press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on macOS) or click the disk icon at the top of the script panel. RStudio will ask you for a filename and a location. Use a meaningful name; for example, 01_setup.R.
To run the code in a script, you have several options:

Run one line at a time. Place the cursor on a line and press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on macOS). RStudio sends that line to the Console for execution.
Run a selected block. Highlight several lines and press Ctrl+Enter. RStudio sends the highlighted block.
Run the entire script. Click “Source” at the top of the script panel, or press Ctrl+Shift+Enter (Cmd+Shift+Enter on macOS).

A script is the most important file type you will create. Most of your work in R will live in scripts. Once a script is saved, you can return to it any time, on any computer that has R, and reproduce exactly what you did.
What a script does not contain: the results of running the code. A script is a recipe, not a meal. To get the results, the recipe has to be cooked again (i.e., run again).
This portability is what makes reproducibility possible in practice. If you share the script together with the data file it was written for, anyone (a collaborator, a reviewer, your future self) can run the script on that data and obtain the same results you did. Exactly the same recipe applied to exactly the same ingredients produces exactly the same meal, every time.
crumbs: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown

title: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown
text:
3.4 The RData file (.RData or .rda)
An RData file is a saved snapshot of objects. It is a binary file (not human-readable when opened in a text editor) with the extension .RData or .rda. It allows you to save objects from your environment to disk, and to load them back later.
There are two common situations.
Saving the entire environment. If you have several objects in your environment and want to save them all at once:

save.image(file = "session_state.RData")

This saves every object currently in the environment into the file session_state.RData (in the current working directory; we will revisit working directories in Chapter 4). To load it back in a future session:

load("session_state.RData")

Every saved object reappears in the environment under its original name.
Saving specific objects. If you only want to save some objects, list them:

save(participants, mean_age, file = "key_values.RData")

This saves only participants and mean_age.
A few comments are worth making here. First, RData files are a convenience, not a substitute for a script. The script is the authoritative record of what you did; the RData file is just a cache of intermediate results. If you ever lose the RData file, the script can recreate it. If you lose the script, the RData file is just a pile of objects with no explanation. Save scripts religiously; save RData files when it would take a long time to recreate the objects (for example, after a long simulation or a slow data import).
Second, RStudio sometimes asks, when you close the program, whether you want to “save the workspace.” This refers to saving the entire environment to a file called .RData in the current working directory, which would then load automatically the next time you open R. We recommend answering No to this prompt, every time. Letting the environment persist invisibly between sessions is a common source of bugs (you cannot tell which objects come from your script and which come from a leftover state). We will return to this in Chapter 4.
crumbs: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown

title: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown
text:
3.5 The R project (.Rproj file)
An R project is a folder on your computer that has been formally designated as a project, by placing a small file with the .Rproj extension inside it. The .Rproj file itself is short and uninteresting; what matters is the structure it imposes on your work.
The mental model is simple: you keep one folder per analysis (or per piece of work) on your computer, and everything related to that analysis lives inside it. The folder typically holds input files (datasets, questionnaires, codebooks), the scripts that operate on those inputs, and the outputs the scripts produce (cleaned datasets, figures, tables, reports). When you turn that folder into an R project, RStudio knows that this folder is the home base for the work, and behaves accordingly.
When you open an R project in RStudio (by double-clicking the .Rproj file, or by going to File > Open Project), four things happen.

RStudio sets the working directory to the project folder. The working directory is the folder R uses as a starting point for finding and saving files. Setting it correctly removes a large class of “file not found” errors.
RStudio loads the project’s settings (which are minimal, but include things like indentation preferences and line endings).
RStudio remembers which scripts you had open the last time you closed the project, and re-opens them.
RStudio starts a fresh R session specific to that project, separate from any other project you might have open in another window.

The most immediately useful of these four things is the first: the working directory. Concretely, suppose your project folder is called 2024_survey and contains a file raw_data.csv. Inside the project, you can read the file with nothing more than its filename:

data <- read.csv("raw_data.csv")

R looks for raw_data.csv relative to the project folder, finds it, and loads it. Saving output works the same way: if your script writes a figure to histogram.png, the file ends up inside the project folder, alongside everything else.
Without an R project, R does not know which folder you are working from, so the same line of code will either fail or load the wrong file. To make it work, you would have to spell out the full path to the file every time, something like:

data <- read.csv("C:/Users/yourname/Documents/research/2024_survey/raw_data.csv")

This is brittle (the path differs between machines, between users, between operating systems) and tedious (every script and every collaborator has to update those paths to match their own setup). With an R project, the short filename raw_data.csv works on any machine that has the project folder.
A second consequence of the project structure is that projects are isolated from one another. You might have one project folder for 2024_survey and another for pilot_study. When you open one, R starts a fresh session, sees only the files in that project’s folder, and does not carry anything over from the other project. Opening a different project starts another fresh session in the other folder. The two analyses cannot accidentally read each other’s files, and changes to the environment in one project have no effect on the other.
The practical effect is that a project keeps everything related to one piece of work in one folder, makes file paths short and portable, and isolates each analysis from every other one. We will discuss projects again in Chapter 4 because they interact with sessions in a way that deserves its own treatment.
R projects are not mandatory. You can work with R by simply saving scripts alongside data files in any folder, without ever creating a .Rproj file. Many people start out that way. But projects are a substantial improvement over the ad hoc setup, and once your work grows past a couple of scripts and a single dataset, the organization that projects impose becomes hard to do without. Your future self will thank your present self for adopting projects early.
To create a project: in the RStudio menu, click File > New Project. A dialog opens with three choices.

New Directory creates a new empty folder on your computer and sets it up as a project.
Existing Directory turns a folder you already have into a project.
Version Control creates a project by cloning a Git or SVN repository (we will not use this for now).

For a beginner, New Directory > New Project is the simplest path. Choose a name (e.g., my_first_project), choose a location on your computer, and click “Create Project.” RStudio creates the folder, places a .Rproj file inside it, and opens the new project. You will see the Files panel pointing at the new (empty) project folder.

3.5.1 Video walkthrough
You may find the following short video helpful for visualizing how to set up and use an R project.

title: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown
text:
3.6 R Markdown (.Rmd)
An R Markdown file is a plain-text file (extension .Rmd) that mixes prose with R code. The prose is written in a simple formatting language called Markdown; the code goes into “chunks” demarcated by special markers. When you “knit” the file, R runs the code, captures the output (numbers, tables, plots), and assembles a finished document (HTML, PDF, or Word) that contains the prose and the results, intermixed.
R Markdown is what you use when you want a document that is also a complete record of an analysis: a lab report, a methods write-up, a thesis chapter, or a journal article.
To create one in RStudio: File > New File > R Markdown. RStudio will pre-fill the file with a small example. Save it with File > Save, run it with the “Knit” button, and a finished document appears.
You will not produce R Markdown documents in Section 1 of this book. They are mentioned here so that the file extension does not surprise you, and so that the conceptual map is complete: a script is for code only, an R Markdown file is for prose plus code with results.
crumbs: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown

title: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown
text:
3.7 Putting the pieces together
A useful summary:

The environment is the in-memory state. It exists only while R is running.
A script (.R) is a saved record of code. It does not contain results.
An RData file (.RData) is a saved snapshot of objects. It contains values, not code.
An R project (.Rproj) is a folder set up to keep one piece of work organized.
An R Markdown file (.Rmd) is a document that mixes prose and code, producing a finished report when rendered.

In a typical research project you will use all of these together: a project folder containing scripts that produce intermediate RData files, with one or more R Markdown files writing up the analysis.
crumbs: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown

title: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown
section: 3.8 Tutorial: create your first project, script, and RData file
text:
3.8 Tutorial: create your first project, script, and RData file
The following is a short hands-on exercise. Doing it once will make the rest of the book easier to follow.

Open RStudio.
Click File > New Project > New Directory > New Project.
Name the directory r_book_practice and place it somewhere convenient (e.g., your Documents folder). Click Create Project.
In the new project, click File > New File > R Script. A blank script opens.
Type the following lines into the script:


participants <- 100
mean_age <- 21.4
condition_labels <- c("control", "treatment")


Save the script with Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on macOS). Name it setup.R. The file should now appear in the Files panel of RStudio.
Run the entire script: click “Source” at the top of the script panel. The three lines execute. Look at the Environment panel: the three objects should now be listed.
Save those three objects to disk:


save.image("setup_state.RData")

A new file, setup_state.RData, appears in your project folder.

Close RStudio entirely. When asked whether to save the workspace, answer No. (We will use the explicit save.image we just ran, not the implicit save-on-close.)
Reopen the project by going to your file browser, navigating to the r_book_practice folder, and double-clicking the .Rproj file. RStudio reopens with that project loaded.
The Environment panel is empty: the previous session is gone. Recover the three objects:


load("setup_state.RData")

The Environment panel now lists the three objects again.
You have just used a project, a script, and an RData file together, and you have seen the difference between code (preserved in the script) and state (preserved in the RData file).
crumbs: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown

title: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown
text:
3.9 Check your understanding
1. What is the “environment” in R?

 A folder on your computer where R is installed. A list of all R packages you have installed. The list of objects R is currently holding in memory during a session. A backup file that R creates automatically when you close it.

2. What happens to the environment when you close R?

 It is automatically saved to the hard drive at all times. It is lost; only saved files (scripts, RData files) persist on disk. It is sent to the R Foundation for safekeeping. It is moved to the Recycle Bin or Trash.

3. Which file type is the most authoritative record of what you did, and should be saved religiously?

 An RData file. An R project file. An R script (.R file). An R Markdown file.

4. What does save.image("session.RData") do?

 It saves all installed packages to disk. It saves the most recent plot to disk. It saves all objects currently in the environment to a single file on disk. It saves the entire R installation to disk.

5. What is the practical purpose of an R project?

 An R project replaces the need for scripts. An R project is a folder formally designated as a project, which sets the working directory and keeps related files together. An R project is a paid subscription service from RStudio. An R project is the same thing as an RData file.

6. Which best describes an R Markdown (.Rmd) file?

 An R Markdown file is a faster version of an R script. An R Markdown file mixes prose and code, and when rendered produces a document containing the prose and the code's output. An R Markdown file is a backup of the R installation. An R Markdown file can only be opened in Microsoft Word.

7. When RStudio asks whether to “save the workspace” on closing, should you say yes?

 Yes, always: it ensures your work is never lost. Yes, but only when working on Windows. No: letting the environment persist invisibly between sessions is a common source of bugs, and you should re-run your script each session instead. It does not matter; the prompt has no effect.
crumbs: 3  Scripts, RData, projects, environments, and R Markdown

title: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions
text:
4.1 Why this chapter exists
Chapter 3 introduced R projects briefly. Chapter 4 returns to them, alongside a related concept (the R session) that often causes confusion. The two are easy to conflate but distinct, and the distinction matters in practice. The promise of this chapter is that, by the end, you will know what is happening when you “restart the session,” when to do it, and how it relates to projects, scripts, and the environment.
crumbs: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions

title: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions
crumbs: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions

title: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions
section: 4.3 How sessions and projects fit together
text:
4.3 How sessions and projects fit together
A project is a folder; a session is a running instance of R. They are different kinds of thing.
Their relationship in RStudio works as follows. Each open project has its own session. If you open a project, RStudio starts a session associated with that project. If you switch to a different project (using File > Open Project), RStudio shuts down the current session and starts a new one in the new project. If you have two projects open in two RStudio windows simultaneously, you have two independent sessions running.
This is convenient: it ensures that the work in one project does not contaminate the work in another. Objects created while working on Project A will not appear when you switch to Project B.
crumbs: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions

title: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions
section: 4.4 Why and when to restart the session
text:
4.4 Why and when to restart the session
Working in an interactive console encourages a habit that, if left unchecked, leads to subtle bugs. Over the course of an hour, you create dozens of objects, load several packages, and make small changes to the code as you go. Some of those objects are stale: they were created earlier in the session and no longer reflect what your current script would produce if run from scratch.
The danger is that your script can appear to work in a particular session because of an object that exists in your environment but is not actually created by the script anywhere. When you open the script tomorrow in a fresh session, the object is gone and the script fails. Worse: someone else (or future you) runs the script and gets a different result, because their session does not have the same accumulated state.
The defense against this is simple: regularly restart the session and re-run the script from the top. A passing script in a clean session is a script that actually works. A passing script in a session you have been using for hours is a script that works in that session, which is a weaker claim.
To restart the session in RStudio: click Session > Restart R, or press Ctrl+Shift+F10 (Cmd+Shift+0 on macOS). All objects disappear, all loaded packages are unloaded, and you start with a clean slate. Now run your script from the top. If it produces the expected results, you have evidence that your script is self-contained.
A reasonable habit is to restart the session at the start of each work session and at any moment when something seems “off.” Some people restart it many times a day; the cost is essentially zero (a fresh session takes a second to start).
crumbs: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions

title: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions
text:
4.5 Saving (and not saving) the environment
In Chapter 3 we recommended answering No to the prompt “Save workspace image?” when closing RStudio. The reasoning is now in scope.
The prompt asks whether you want to save the entire environment to a file called .RData in the project folder, which would automatically reload the next time you open R. If you answer Yes, what happens is this. The next time you open the project, the previous session’s environment is silently restored. Your Environment panel will be full of objects from yesterday. None of those objects are produced by your current script; they are leftovers. Your script will appear to work, because the objects it expects are already there, regardless of whether the script actually creates them.
Recall the recipe analogy from Chapter 3: the script is the recipe, the data is the ingredients, and running the script is cooking the meal. In that picture, letting R restore the previous workspace is like cooking a new dish in a pot that still contains leftovers from yesterday’s meal, without washing it first. Sometimes those leftovers do not affect the new dish; other times they spoil it in ways that are hard to detect. The safe habit is the same in both cases: clean the pot (or the workspace) before starting something new.
This is precisely the failure mode described in the previous section, made worse by being invisible. You did not even notice that the objects had been preserved.
The recommended setting is to disable this entirely. In RStudio:

Open Tools > Global Options.
Click the General tab.
Under “Workspace,” uncheck “Restore .RData into workspace at startup.”
Set “Save workspace to .RData on exit” to Never.
Click OK.

With these settings, every R session starts clean. Your script is the only source of objects in the environment. If you find that you need to preserve an expensive intermediate result, save it explicitly with save() (as we did in Chapter 3) and load it explicitly with load() at the top of the script that needs it.
crumbs: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions

title: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions
section: 4.6 Working directory: where R looks for files
text:
4.6 Working directory: where R looks for files
When you ask R to read a file, e.g. read.csv("data.csv"), R looks for data.csv in the working directory. The working directory is a setting of the current session: it points at one folder on your computer, and that folder is the implicit “current location” for any file operation that does not specify a full path.
To find out what the working directory currently is:

getwd()

When you open an R project, the working directory is set to the project folder automatically. This is one of the main practical benefits of using projects: file paths in your scripts can be relative to the project folder, which makes the scripts portable. A line like read.csv("data/survey.csv") will work on any computer that has the project folder, because the path is resolved relative to the project, not relative to a specific user’s hard drive.
If you are not using a project, the working directory defaults to a system folder (your home directory on macOS and Linux, or “Documents” on Windows). You can change it manually:

setwd("C:/Users/yourname/Documents/r_practice")

We recommend not using setwd() in scripts. If a script contains an explicit path, the script becomes tied to that one computer. Use a project, and let the working directory be set by the project’s location.
crumbs: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions

title: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions
section: 4.7 Tutorial: practice opening, restarting, and switching
text:
4.7 Tutorial: practice opening, restarting, and switching
This tutorial assumes you completed the tutorial at the end of Chapter 3 (creating the r_book_practice project with a setup.R script and a setup_state.RData file).
Part A: Open a project from a file browser.

Close RStudio entirely.
Open your operating system’s file browser (Windows Explorer or macOS Finder).
Navigate to the r_book_practice folder.
Find the .Rproj file. Double-click it. RStudio opens, the project is loaded, and setup.R may already be open if you had it open last time.
Look at the title bar of the RStudio window. It should display the project name. Look at the Files panel: it points at the project folder.

Part B: Confirm that the environment is empty in a new session.

Look at the Environment panel. If you set “Restore .RData into workspace at startup” to unchecked (as recommended above), it should be empty. If it shows the objects from your previous session, your global options still allow restoration; revisit the steps in “Saving (and not saving) the environment” above.

Part C: Restart the session deliberately.

Run your script: open setup.R, click “Source.” The three objects appear in the Environment panel.
Click Session > Restart R. The Console clears, the Environment panel empties, and a fresh session begins.
Run the script again. The three objects reappear.
This is the workflow you want as a default. Anything that exists in the environment exists because the script put it there.

Part D: Switch projects.

Click File > New Project > New Directory > New Project. Create a second project called r_book_practice_two somewhere convenient.
RStudio shuts down the previous session, opens the new project, and starts a fresh session. The Environment panel is empty.
Click File > Open Project and navigate back to the original r_book_practice project. RStudio shuts down the second session and reopens the first. Notice that the Environment panel is empty again, even though you previously had objects in it: each open of a project starts a brand-new session.
To recover the objects from the saved RData file: load("setup_state.RData"). The objects reappear.

This pattern (open project, run script, restart when uncertain, save expensive intermediate results explicitly) is the foundation of a clean R workflow.
crumbs: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions

title: 4  Working with R projects and R sessions
text:
4.8 Check your understanding
1. What is an R session?

 A folder on the hard drive that R writes log files to. One running instance of R, which holds the environment, loaded packages, and current settings. A subscription service from RStudio. Another name for an R Markdown document.

2. What happens to the environment when an R session ends?

 Saved to disk in the project folder. Compressed and emailed to you. Lost: the environment, loaded packages, and any in-memory state are all destroyed. Backed up automatically to the cloud.

3. Why do experienced R users recommend regularly restarting the session?

 Restarting clears the working directory but keeps all objects in memory. Restarting starts a fresh session, ensuring that your script works on its own without depending on stale objects accumulated during the session. Restarting reinstalls R, removing all packages. Restarting is a way to upgrade RStudio.

4. Should you let RStudio automatically restore the previous workspace at startup?

 It is recommended, because it speeds up startup. It is discouraged, because it silently restores stale objects from the previous session, which can cause bugs and obscure the source of the objects in the environment. It is the only way to preserve your data between sessions. It is required by reproducibility journals.

5. What is the working directory?

 It is the folder where R itself was installed. It is the folder R uses as the implicit current location for file operations that do not specify a full path. It is the folder where RStudio stores user account information. It is the folder where R Markdown files are automatically rendered.

6. Should you use setwd() to set the working directory in your scripts?

 Yes, every script should begin with setwd("C:/Users/...") to be safe. No: hard-coding paths makes the script tied to one computer; using an R project lets paths be relative to the project folder. It is irrelevant; R does not have a working directory. Only on Linux.

7. How costly is it to restart the R session?

 Restarting is destructive: you should restart only after a crash. Restarting is essentially free (a fresh session takes about a second), and a regular habit of restarting catches problems early. Restarting requires re-installing all packages each time. Restarting is reserved for emergencies.

title: 5  Objects and functions
text:
5.1 The two main verbs of R
In Chapter 1 we said that working in R consists mostly of two activities: creating objects, and feeding objects into operations to produce new objects. The operations themselves are called functions. This chapter takes that loose description and replaces it with a more precise vocabulary.
Concretely, this chapter covers:

title: 5  Objects and functions
text:
The kinds of objects R has (values, vectors, data frames, and a few related types).
The fact that some objects are composed of smaller objects, and how to look inside them.
What a function is and how it works in practice.
How to assign objects, read what is inside them, and extract pieces of them.

title: 5  Objects and functions
text:
5.2 Single values
The simplest kind of object in R is a single value. A number, a single piece of text, or a true/false flag are all single values.
To create a single value, you use the assignment arrow <-. The arrow points from the value to the name. The general form is name <- value.

participants <- 100
mean_age <- 21.4
study_name <- "pilot 2024"
finished <- TRUE

You have created four objects. The first two are numbers. The third is a piece of text, called a character string or just string. Strings are written between double quotes. The fourth is a logical value (TRUE or FALSE), used for true/false flags.
To inspect an object, type its name in the Console:

participants
# returns 100

R prints the value. (Throughout this book, comments starting with # indicate what R returns, so that you can read the examples without running them.)
R has different “types” for these different kinds of values: numeric for numbers, character for strings, logical for true/false. To check the type of an object:

class(participants)   # returns "numeric"
class(study_name)     # returns "character"
class(finished)       # returns "logical"

The function class() is itself an example of what we will discuss later in the chapter: a function that takes an object as input and returns information about it.

title: 5  Objects and functions
text:
5.3 Vectors
A vector is an ordered sequence of values of the same type. In R, a vector is created with the function c() (the letter “c” stands for “combine”):

ages <- c(19, 22, 21, 25, 18, 30, 27)
genders <- c("F", "M", "F", "F", "M", "F", "M")
finished_each <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)

ages is now a vector of seven numbers, genders is a vector of seven strings, and finished_each is a vector of seven logical values. The objects you created with single values in the previous section were technically vectors of length one; R does not formally distinguish “scalars” from “vectors of length one.” Almost everything in R is a vector at some level.
To find the length of a vector, use length():

length(ages)
# returns 7

To extract one or more elements of a vector, use square brackets [ ]:

ages[1]        # the first element
ages[3]        # the third element
ages[c(1, 3)]  # the first and third elements together
ages[1:5]      # elements one through five

Note that R uses 1-based indexing: the first element is at position 1, not 0. (If you have used Python or some other languages, this is one of the differences to remember.)
The expression 1:5 is shorthand for the vector c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5). The colon operator generates a sequence of consecutive integers.
A common mistake is to mix types within c(). R will silently convert all elements to the most general type:

mixed <- c(1, 2, "three")
class(mixed)
# returns "character"

The first two values were converted to strings ("1" and "2") so that all elements have a common type. This is rarely what you want; if you find yourself doing this by accident, it usually means you misclassified the data on input.
In practice, at the beginner level you will rarely create vectors by hand with c(). Most of the time you will be working with vectors that came from a real data file (a CSV, a survey export, a spreadsheet). What matters at this stage is that you understand what a vector is and how to manipulate one: how to find its length, how to pull out specific elements with square brackets, and how it behaves when types are mixed. Those skills transfer directly to vectors that arrive in your environment from outside.

title: 5  Objects and functions
text:
5.4 Data frames
A data frame is the structure most often used to represent a dataset: rows are observations (e.g., participants), columns are variables (e.g., age, gender, response on item 1). It is the R analogue of a spreadsheet.
You can create a data frame from existing vectors:

participants_data <- data.frame(
  id     = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7),
  age    = c(19, 22, 21, 25, 18, 30, 27),
  gender = c("F", "M", "F", "F", "M", "F", "M"),
  finished = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
)

Now participants_data is a data frame with seven rows and four columns. To see it:

participants_data

To learn its dimensions:

nrow(participants_data)   # 7
ncol(participants_data)   # 4
dim(participants_data)    # both at once: c(7, 4)

To peek at the first few rows:

head(participants_data)        # first 6 rows by default
head(participants_data, n = 3) # first 3 rows
tail(participants_data, n = 3) # last 3 rows

To get a structural overview:

str(participants_data)

str() (for “structure”) prints a compact summary: the number of observations, the number of variables, the type of each variable, and a few sample values.
To extract one column of a data frame, use the dollar sign $:

participants_data$age
# returns the vector c(19, 22, 21, 25, 18, 30, 27)

participants_data$age returns the column age as a regular vector. You can do anything with it that you would do with any other vector:

mean(participants_data$age)
# returns 23.14286

You can also extract rows and columns by position with two-dimensional bracket indexing. The general form is dataframe[rows, columns]:

participants_data[1, ]            # first row, all columns
participants_data[, 2]            # all rows, second column
participants_data[1:3, c(1, 2)]   # first three rows, first two columns

Leaving one of the slots empty means “all”: [1, ] means “row 1, all columns,” and [, 2] means “all rows, column 2.” This pattern is worth practicing; it is used frequently.
As with vectors, at the beginner level you will rarely create data frames by hand. Most of the time you will load a data frame from a real data file (a CSV, an SPSS file, an Excel sheet) using a function like read.csv(). What matters at this stage is that you understand what a data frame is, how to inspect its structure, and how to pull out specific columns, rows, and individual cells. Those skills are exactly what you will use on real datasets.

title: 5  Objects and functions
text:
5.5 Objects composed of objects
We have already seen this idea in passing, but it is worth making explicit. A vector is a sequence of single values. A data frame is a collection of vectors of equal length. A data frame, in turn, is itself an object that can be passed as input to functions like nrow(), mean(), str(). Larger objects are built from smaller ones.
Two more compound types are worth knowing about, even though we will not use them heavily in Section 1.
A list is an ordered collection of objects, like a vector, except that the elements can be of any type and any length. A list could contain a single number in the first slot, a vector of strings in the second slot, and a data frame in the third slot. Many functions that fit statistical models (regressions, ANOVAs) return their results as a list. We will revisit lists when we encounter such results in later sections.
A factor is a vector of strings that R has been told to treat as a fixed set of categorical levels. Factors are useful for categorical predictors in models (e.g., experimental conditions). For now, what matters is to recognize the term when you see it.
Whenever an object is composed of named parts, the dollar sign $ is the operator you use to look at, or extract, one of those parts. We saw this in the previous section, where participants_data$age returned the age column of a data frame. The same operator works on lists: if model_results is a list with a named slot called coefficients, then model_results$coefficients returns the contents of that slot. The pattern is always the same: write the name of the outer object, a dollar sign, and the name of the inner part you want.

participants_data$age          # the age column of a data frame
model_results$coefficients     # the coefficients slot of a model-results list

You will use $ constantly when working with real data and with the output of analysis functions. Most of those outputs are composed objects whose useful pieces have names; $ is the way you reach them.

title: 5  Objects and functions
text:
5.6 Functions
A function is a piece of R that takes objects as input and produces a new object as output. We have already used several: mean(), class(), length(), nrow(), c(), data.frame(). The general form of a function call is:
function_name(input1, input2, ...)
The inputs are called arguments. The general syntax is to write the function name, an open parenthesis, the arguments separated by commas, and a close parenthesis. R passes the arguments to the function, the function does its work, and a value is returned. That returned value can be used (assigned to a name, passed to another function, printed).
A useful mental model is a machine in a factory: ingredients go in, the machine processes them, and a product comes out. R’s functions are exactly this. The “ingredients” are the objects you pass in, the “machine” is the body of the function, and the “product” is the returned object.
Here is the same function, mean, used in three different ways:

mean(ages)                          # used directly; result printed
average_age <- mean(ages)           # result assigned to a name
mean(participants_data$age)         # input pulled from a data frame using $

The third line uses the dollar sign $ introduced in the previous section: participants_data$age extracts the age column from the data frame and passes it directly to mean(), with no intermediate object. Reading this kind of expression from the inside out is a useful habit: first participants_data$age produces a vector, then mean() takes that vector and returns a single number.
Many functions accept multiple arguments. round(), for example, takes a number and an optional second argument specifying how many decimals to keep:

round(23.14286)            # 23
round(23.14286, digits = 2) # 23.14

The phrase digits = 2 is called a named argument: you are explicitly identifying which argument you are setting. You can also pass arguments by position (round(23.14286, 2)), but for any argument other than the first one or two, named arguments are clearer and less error-prone.
Every function has a help page. To open the help page for a function, type ? followed by its name in the Console:

?mean
?round
?data.frame

The help page lists the arguments, what they do, what the function returns, and usually a few examples at the bottom. Reading help pages is a skill that takes some getting used to. The examples are the most useful section for beginners; if you are unsure how to use a function, scroll directly to the bottom of its help page.

title: 5  Objects and functions
text:
5.7 Looking inside objects
A small set of functions are constantly useful for “looking inside” objects:

class(x)        # what type of object is x?
length(x)       # how long is it?
str(x)          # a structural overview
head(x)         # the first few elements (or rows)
summary(x)      # a quick summary, type-dependent
names(x)        # the names of components, if any

For data frames specifically, you will also use:

nrow(df)        # number of rows
ncol(df)        # number of columns
colnames(df)    # column names

When you encounter an unfamiliar object (for example, the result of a function you have not used before), running class() and str() on it is a good first move. Together they tell you what kind of object you have and what is inside it.

title: 5  Objects and functions
text:
5.8 Exercises
Below are some exercises you can do in RStudio. They are not graded; the answers will appear in your Console as you work. The aim is to get you comfortable with assigning, inspecting, and indexing objects.
Exercise 1: assignment. Create three objects:

n_items containing the integer 10
scale_name containing the string “Big Five”
responses containing the vector c(3, 5, 4, 2, 5, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4)

Inspect each by typing its name in the Console.
Exercise 2: type-checking. For each of the three objects above, run class(). What does each return?
Exercise 3: indexing. From responses, extract:

the first element
the last element (hint: use length(responses) inside the brackets)
elements 1 through 5
elements 6 through 10

Exercise 4: a data frame. Create a data frame with three rows and three columns:

mini_data <- data.frame(
  id     = c(1, 2, 3),
  rt_ms  = c(523, 612, 478),
  correct = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
)

Then:

print the data frame;
run str(mini_data);
extract the column rt_ms as a vector;
extract the second row;
extract the cell in row 1, column 2.

Exercise 5: functions. Compute the mean of responses and assign it to an object called mean_response. Then compute the mean of mini_data$rt_ms and assign it to mean_rt.
Exercise 6: help pages. Open the help page for mean (with ?mean). Find the description of the argument na.rm. What does it do? (You will encounter this argument frequently when you work with real data, where missing values are common.)

title: 5  Objects and functions
text:
5.9 Check your understanding
1. What is a vector in R?

 A vector with mixed types: numbers, strings, and logicals together. Another name for the working directory. An ordered sequence of values of the same type, created with c(). A built-in plotting function.

2. At what index is the first element of a vector in R?

 Index 0. Index 1. Index -1. It depends on the operating system.

3. What is a data frame?

 A spreadsheet file saved in CSV format. A two-dimensional structure where rows are observations and columns are variables, holding vectors of equal length. A list of installed packages. A graphical representation of a dataset.

4. Which expression extracts the column age from a data frame called participants_data?

 participants_data[age] participants_data#age participants_data$age participants_data->age

5. What is a function?

 A type of file used to save analyses. A panel in the RStudio interface. A piece of R that takes objects as input and produces a new object as output. A specific kind of vector.

6. What does round(23.14286, digits = 2) do?

 Add a new column called digits to the data frame. Round 23.14286 to two decimals, returning 23.14. Round 23.14286 to two significant figures, returning 23. Multiply 23.14286 by 2.

7. If ages is a vector of length 7, what does length(ages) return?

 It returns 0 because R indexes from 0. It returns 1 because there is one element. It returns 7, the length of the original vector. It causes an error.

8. What does typing ?mean in the Console do?

 Open the documentation for the mean package. Open the help page for the mean function, listing its arguments and examples. Calculate the mean of all objects in the environment. Print the source code of the mean function.

title: 6  Basic operations, custom functions, and packages
text:
6.1 Overview
This chapter is the longest in Section 1. It is also the chapter where the value of working in R, as opposed to working in SPSS or Excel, becomes most concrete. The chapter is organized in four parts:
A note before we begin. We introduce custom functions in this chapter only for illustration. In the rest of Section 1 and the early sections that follow, you will not need to write your own functions. There are tens of thousands of functions already written by other people, and most of your learning curve will be about finding them and using them. We will return to writing your own functions much later in the book, once you are comfortable using existing ones.

title: 6  Basic operations, custom functions, and packages
text:
Basic operations: assignment, arithmetic, and the small set of summary functions you will use most often (mean, sd, min, max, median).
A first look at custom functions: how you would package a few of those operations into a single named operation, illustrated with a deliberately simple example using if and else.
A substantive example: a survey dataset whose variables have been distorted by a software bug, walked through three times: manually, with a function applied repeatedly, and with a function applied in a single line. This is the example that shows what coding actually buys you.
Packages: what they are, how to install and load them, and how to find documentation. Most of the functions you will use in your career are in packages, not in base R.

title: 6  Basic operations, custom functions, and packages
text:
6.2 Basic operations

6.2.1 Assignment
You assign a value to a name with the arrow <-:

x <- 5
y <- 12
participants <- 100

The arrow is read “gets”: “x gets 5.” You can also use =, but <- is the convention in R, and it removes ambiguity in places where = has another meaning (notably inside function calls, where = is used for named arguments).


6.2.2 Arithmetic
R supports the usual arithmetic operators:

x + y     # addition: 17
x - y     # subtraction: -7
x * y     # multiplication: 60
x / y     # division: 0.4166667
x^2       # exponentiation: 25
y %% 5    # remainder ("modulo"): 2
y %/% 5   # integer division: 2

These work on vectors as well as on single values. When applied to a vector, the operation is done element-wise:

ages <- c(19, 22, 21, 25, 18, 30, 27)
ages + 10
# returns c(29, 32, 31, 35, 28, 40, 37)
ages / 2
# returns c(9.5, 11.0, 10.5, 12.5, 9.0, 15.0, 13.5)

When two vectors of the same length are combined, the operation is applied element-wise:

v1 <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
v2 <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
v1 + v2
# returns c(11, 22, 33, 44)



6.2.3 Summary functions
The functions you will use most often when you first look at a vector of numbers are:

sum(ages)      # total
mean(ages)     # arithmetic mean
median(ages)   # median
min(ages)      # smallest value
max(ages)      # largest value
range(ages)    # min and max returned together as a vector of length 2
sd(ages)       # standard deviation (using n - 1)
var(ages)      # variance (using n - 1)
length(ages)   # number of elements

And the very useful catch-all:

summary(ages)
# returns Min., 1st Qu., Median, Mean, 3rd Qu., Max.

summary() is type-aware. On a numeric vector you get the six-number summary above. On a logical vector you get counts of TRUE and FALSE. On a data frame, you get a one-column summary for each column.
A single practical caveat: if any value in the vector is missing (NA), most of these functions return NA by default. To compute over the non-missing values only, set the na.rm argument to TRUE:

ages_with_na <- c(19, 22, NA, 25, 18, 30, 27)
mean(ages_with_na)              # returns NA
mean(ages_with_na, na.rm = TRUE) # returns 23.5

You will encounter na.rm = TRUE constantly in real data analysis, because real data has missing values.

title: 6  Basic operations, custom functions, and packages
section: 6.3 A first look at custom functions
text:
6.3 A first look at custom functions
Suppose you frequently want to look at five summaries of a vector at once: the mean, the standard deviation, the median, the minimum, and the maximum. You could write the five lines every time:

mean(ages)
sd(ages)
median(ages)
min(ages)
max(ages)

This is tedious. A custom function lets you bundle those lines into one named operation.
Here is the simplest possible version:

quick_summary <- function(x) {
  cat("Mean:   ", mean(x), "\n")
  cat("SD:     ", sd(x), "\n")
  cat("Median: ", median(x), "\n")
  cat("Min:    ", min(x), "\n")
  cat("Max:    ", max(x), "\n")
}

Read this carefully. The structure of every function definition in R is the same:
function_name <- function(arguments) {
  body
}
function_name <- function(...) says “create a function and give it a name.” The arguments listed in the parentheses are the inputs. The body, between the curly braces, is the code that runs when the function is called. (cat() is a small function that prints text to the Console; "\n" is a newline character that puts the next item on its own line.)
To use the new function, call it like any other function:

quick_summary(ages)

The function runs its body on ages, prints five lines, and returns nothing further.
We can make the function slightly more careful by adding a check. Suppose we want it to refuse non-numeric input rather than producing a confusing error from mean(). We can use if and else:

quick_summary <- function(x) {
  if (!is.numeric(x)) {
    cat("Input is not numeric; quick_summary cannot run.\n")
  } else {
    cat("Mean:   ", mean(x), "\n")
    cat("SD:     ", sd(x), "\n")
    cat("Median: ", median(x), "\n")
    cat("Min:    ", min(x), "\n")
    cat("Max:    ", max(x), "\n")
  }
}

is.numeric(x) returns TRUE if x is numeric and FALSE otherwise. !is.numeric(x) reverses this; the ! means “not.” So the if statement is read: “if x is not numeric, print a warning; else, print the five summaries.”
You now have a tiny function with a guard clause. Call it on a numeric vector and you get the summaries; call it on a string vector and you get the warning:

quick_summary(ages)
quick_summary(c("a", "b", "c"))

This is intentionally a small example. We are not yet using any of the more powerful tools R has for writing functions; in particular, we are not using the “apply” family of functions, which we will introduce much later. For now, the goal is for you to recognize the structure of a function definition when you see it, not to write your own.
