title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.1 Overview
Up to this point we have looked at our data through numbers: counts, means, standard deviations, residuals. Numbers compress information, which is useful when you want a single value to compare or to put in a sentence. But numbers also hide information, and what they hide can change the answer to a research question.
This chapter is about the other half of looking at data: visualization. The chapter does not contain plotting code yet. The reason is deliberate: it is much easier to learn the how of plotting once you know the what and the why. We start with the questions a good plot answers, the conceptual framework that organizes every plot you will ever make, the principles that distinguish a good plot from a bad one, and the kinds of judgment calls you will face when reading or making one. The tools to translate these decisions into actual plots in R come in the next chapter.
The plots that appear throughout this chapter are produced with ggplot2, the R package you will learn in the next chapter. The code for each plot is hidden for now, so you can focus on the visual outcome rather than the syntax. You will revisit these examples and reproduce them yourself once you have learned the package.
crumbs: 10  First principles of data visualization

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.2 Why visualize?
A famous example illustrates the problem with relying on summary statistics alone. Anscombe’s quartet is a set of four small datasets, constructed by the statistician Frank Anscombe in 1973, that have nearly identical summary statistics. The quartet is built into R, so you can inspect it directly:

data("anscombe")
anscombe

The data frame has eight columns: four x columns (x1, x2, x3, x4) and four corresponding y columns (y1, y2, y3, y4). Each (x, y) pair is one of the four datasets. Each dataset has 11 observations.
Compute the means of all eight columns:

sapply(anscombe, mean)
# x1 x2 x3 x4   y1   y2   y3   y4
#  9  9  9  9 7.50 7.50 7.50 7.50

All four x means are 9.0 and all four y means are 7.50. The four standard deviations agree to two decimals as well, and the four correlation coefficients between x and y are all approximately 0.82. If you compute the line of best fit (the regression line) for each pair, all four lines are essentially the same.
By every numerical summary you can think of at this point, the four datasets are interchangeable.
When you plot them, they look completely different.









Dataset 1 is a clean, roughly linear relationship. Dataset 2 is a smooth curve where a straight line is the wrong model entirely. Dataset 3 is a near-perfect linear relationship plus one extreme outlier that pulls the regression line away from the true pattern. Dataset 4 is a vertical line of constant x with one isolated point at a very different x; that single point is what creates the apparent correlation.
Four datasets, four very different stories, identical summary statistics. The lesson Anscombe drew, and the one this book takes seriously, is short: always plot your data. Numerical summaries do not protect you from misreading what is actually in the dataset.
A good visualization does things that numbers alone cannot:

It reveals the shape of a distribution (symmetric? skewed? bimodal?).
It shows the relationship between variables (linear? curved? no pattern?).
It exposes outliers and unusual observations.
It communicates findings to others quickly and intuitively, in a way that a table of numbers cannot.

Here is a video from YouTube that explains two uses of data visualization:
crumbs: 10  First principles of data visualization

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.3 The grammar of graphics
Most modern data-visualization systems (including ggplot2, the R package you will learn in the next chapter) are based on a framework called the grammar of graphics, formalized by the statistician Leland Wilkinson. The core idea is that any plot is built from the same three ingredients, combined in different ways.









Data. The dataset you want to visualize. Without data there is nothing to plot. The data are usually a data frame.
Aesthetics. A mapping from variables in the data to visual properties of the plot. Examples: the x-axis represents hours_weekly; the y-axis represents aggression; the color of each point represents condition; the size of each point represents age. Each aesthetic mapping turns one variable into one visual channel.
Geometry. The visual shape used to represent each observation. Examples: points (a scatterplot), bars (a bar chart), lines (a line chart), boxes (a boxplot), tiles (a heatmap).
By choosing data, aesthetics, and a geometry, you specify the plot. The grammar is called a “grammar” by analogy with language: just as a finite vocabulary plus a set of rules generates an unbounded number of sentences, a finite set of aesthetics and geometries plus a dataset generates an unbounded number of plots.
This vocabulary will become concrete the moment you write your first ggplot2 line. The point of introducing it now is that plots are not arbitrary collections of marks on a page. They are the result of three explicit decisions, and you can usually improve a bad plot by going back and rethinking one of the three.
crumbs: 10  First principles of data visualization

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
section: 10.4 Seven principles of good data visualization
text:
10.4 Seven principles of good data visualization
Reasonable people disagree about details, but the field has converged on a small set of principles. The seven that follow are the most consequential for the kinds of plots you will make as a researcher. We state each one as a directive and then explain it.

10.4.1 1. Show the data, not just summaries
A bar chart that displays only the group means is a bar chart that hides the individual observations. The reader cannot tell whether the difference between groups reflects a consistent difference across all participants or a small number of extreme participants pulling the mean in one direction. Whenever possible, show the individual data points (for example, as a scatter or jittered dots) in addition to any summary statistic, or use a geometry like a boxplot or violin plot that displays the distribution rather than collapsing it to a single number.
Bad example. A bar chart of group means, with no indication of within-group variability or individual scores.









Good example. The same group means, with all individual scores overlaid as jittered points. Now the reader sees the spread within each group and can judge whether the difference in means reflects a consistent shift or a few extreme scores.











10.4.2 2. Choose the right geometry for the data type
The right geometry depends on what kind of variables you have:

One continuous variable, distribution. Use a histogram or a density plot. These show the shape of the distribution: where it is centered, how spread out it is, whether it is symmetric or skewed, whether it has a single peak or multiple peaks.
One categorical variable, counts. Use a bar chart. Each bar represents a category; the bar height represents the count or proportion in that category.
Two continuous variables, relationship. Use a scatterplot. Each observation is one point; the relationship between the variables (linear, curved, none) becomes visible at a glance.
One continuous variable across one categorical variable, group comparison. Use a boxplot, a violin plot, or overlaid histograms. These show how the distribution of the continuous variable differs across groups.

There are more advanced choices for more complicated questions, but the four above cover most of what you will plot.
Bad example. A bar chart used to display the relationship between two continuous variables (hours_weekly and aggression). Bar charts are designed for categorical comparisons; using one here forces a continuous variable into discrete bars and discards the relationship.









Good example. A scatterplot. Each participant is one point; the relationship (or absence of one) is visible directly.











10.4.3 3. Label everything clearly
Every axis needs a label. The label should describe the variable in plain language (“Aggression Score (1-10)”), not the column name from the dataset (aggression). If you use color or shape to encode a variable, include a legend that explains what each color or shape means. Give the plot a title that states what it shows. A reader who sees the plot for the first time, with no other context, should be able to identify what is being shown.
Bad example. A scatterplot with no title, default axis labels (the raw column names), and no legend explanation. A reader without context cannot tell what is being shown.









Good example. Same plot with a descriptive title, plain-language axis labels, and a legend identifying the conditions.











10.4.4 4. Avoid chart junk
The term chart junk was popularized by the statistician Edward Tufte. It refers to visual elements that do not encode information: unnecessary gridlines, 3D effects on a 2D plot, decorative images, drop shadows, gradient fills, excessive colors. Chart junk distracts the reader from the actual data and signals carelessness. Every element on a plot should serve a purpose. If you can remove an element without losing information, remove it.
Bad example. The same data, encrusted with chart junk: gradient bars, dark gridlines, heavy borders, oversaturated colors.









Good example. Same data, with everything that does not encode information removed. The bars are the only visual element with weight; the eye goes directly to the comparison.











10.4.5 5. Do not mislead with scales
The scale of an axis controls how big a difference looks on the page. A small difference in y-values can be made to look enormous by truncating the y-axis to start near the data values rather than at zero. The classic example: bars that visually look twice as tall but actually differ by 0.1 on a scale of 1 to 10, because the y-axis has been truncated to range from 4.0 to 6.0 instead of 0 to 10. This is misleading and you should not do it.
Two related rules. Do not use dual y-axes. A plot with two different y-axes (one on the left, one on the right) almost always misleads, because the reader cannot tell which line corresponds to which axis without effort, and the apparent relationship between the lines depends entirely on how the two axes are scaled. Use consistent scales when comparing plots. If you show two plots side by side, the reader will compare them visually; using different scales for the same variable will mislead.
Bad example. The y-axis is truncated to range from 4.0 to 6.0. The two bars look dramatically different in height; the visual impression is that the violent condition produced an enormous effect.









Good example. Same data, y-axis on its natural scale (1 to 10). The difference between conditions is real and interpretable, but it is not visually inflated.











10.4.6 6. Avoid pie charts
Pie charts ask the reader to compare the angles of slices, and humans are demonstrably bad at comparing angles. Comparing the heights of bars is much easier and more accurate. Almost every situation in which someone reaches for a pie chart is better served by a bar chart. There are a few special cases (a pie with two or three slices when the goal is to communicate “this small slice versus everything else”), but the default should be a bar chart.
Bad example. A pie chart of gender counts. Comparing slices by angle is harder than reading bar heights.









Good example. Same data as a bar chart. The differences in counts are immediate.











10.4.7 7. Use color purposefully
Color in a plot should encode information, not decorate it. Each distinct color should mean something specific (one experimental condition, one category of participants, one variable). Use a small number of colors; a plot with ten colors is a plot the reader cannot interpret.
A practical detail: roughly 8 percent of men and 0.5 percent of women have some form of color-vision deficiency, most commonly red-green confusion. Plots that distinguish groups by red versus green are unreadable for those readers. Use color palettes designed to be colorblind-friendly (any modern plotting library, including ggplot2, provides such palettes), and where possible reinforce color with a second visual channel like shape or line type, so the plot remains interpretable even for readers who cannot distinguish the colors.
Bad example. Each participant has been given a different rainbow color for no reason. The colors do not encode anything; they are pure decoration. The reader gets no information from them and the plot is harder to read than the same plot in one color.









Good example. Color is used to encode the experimental condition (the variable the reader actually wants to compare), with a colorblind-safe palette (blue and orange).
crumbs: 10  First principles of data visualization

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.5 Applying the principles
The principles are abstract; they become useful when you apply them to a specific plot. The following five short scenarios illustrate the kind of judgment a careful researcher makes when reading or designing a visualization.
Scenario 1. A researcher wants to show how aggression scores are distributed across all 120 participants. Two options: (a) a bar chart showing the mean aggression score as a single bar, or (b) a histogram showing the distribution of all 120 aggression scores. The histogram is more informative. A single bar tells you one number (the mean). The histogram shows the shape of the distribution, the spread, possible outliers, and any clustering. The bar discards 119 numbers; the histogram keeps them. Principle 1 in action.


















Scenario 2. A researcher wants to compare aggression between the violent and neutral conditions. He produces a bar chart with two bars (one per condition) showing the group means. What is missing? At least three things. The plot does not show the spread of scores within each condition (so you cannot tell whether the difference between groups is large relative to within-group variation). It does not show the individual data points (so you cannot tell whether the difference is driven by all participants or by a few extreme ones). It does not show the shape of the within-group distributions (so you cannot tell whether either group is skewed or has outliers). Better alternatives: overlay the individual data points on the bars; use a boxplot or violin plot per condition; or show the distribution as overlaid histograms. Each of these shows the data, not just the summaries.




































Scenario 3. A researcher wants to examine whether there is a relationship between weekly playing hours (a continuous variable) and aggression (a continuous variable). Which geometry is most appropriate? A scatterplot. Each participant becomes one point at the (hours_weekly, aggression) coordinates, and the relationship (positive, negative, none, linear, curved) is visible directly. A bar chart is wrong because both variables are continuous; a pie chart is wrong because the question is not about proportions; a boxplot is wrong because neither variable is categorical.




































Scenario 4. Suppose you have the same data displayed two ways: option A is a boxplot with one box per condition, with individual data points overlaid; option B is a small table reporting “Violent: M = 5.56, SD = 1.66; Neutral: M = 4.21, SD = 1.24.” Both convey the same basic information. When is the plot better, and when is the table better? The plot is better when you want to communicate to a broad audience, when you want the reader to see the distribution rather than just the summary, and when you suspect the distributions might be unusual (skewed, bimodal, with outliers) and want the reader to check that for themselves. The table is better when you need exact numbers (for reporting in a paper), when the audience is technically sophisticated and prefers precision, or when you have many groups and a plot would become cluttered. In practice, good scientific communication often uses both: a plot for pattern, a table or in-text numbers for precision.










Option B: summary table


Condition
M
SD




Violent
5.56
1.66


Neutral
4.21
1.24



Scenario 5. A researcher plots aggression on the y-axis (the variable ranges from 1 to 10) but sets the y-axis limits to 4.0 to 6.0. The bars for the two conditions now appear dramatically different in height. What is wrong with this? The truncated y-axis visually exaggerates the difference. The actual difference between the two condition means (about 1.35 points on a 1-to-10 scale) is real and worth reporting, but it is not as large as the truncated plot makes it look. The fix is to start the y-axis at the natural minimum of the scale, or at least to show enough of the range that the difference is in proper proportion. If the difference is small relative to the scale of the variable, that is itself a finding and should not be visually inflated. Principle 5 in action.
crumbs: 10  First principles of data visualization

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.6 The wrangle, describe, visualize workflow
You now have three skills that work together:

Data wrangling (Chapters 8 and 9): getting the data into the right shape, selecting the variables you need, filtering to the rows that are relevant, creating derived variables.
Descriptive statistics (Chapter 9): summarizing the data numerically, with summary(), mean(), psych::describe(), or a custom summarize() pipeline.
Data visualization (this chapter, conceptually; the next chapter, in code): communicating patterns visually.

The order in practice is almost always: wrangle first (clean, filter, reshape), then describe (compute summaries to check what you have), then visualize (plot what looks important). Wrangling is usually the largest time investment and the least visible step in a finished paper. Descriptives are how you sanity-check the wrangling. Visualization is how you discover what is worth modeling and how you communicate the results once you have modeled them.
crumbs: 10  First principles of data visualization

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.7 Looking ahead
The next chapter introduces ggplot2, the package that lets you implement the principles of this chapter in actual R code. ggplot2 is the visualization component of the tidyverse you loaded in Chapter 9, so you do not need to install anything new. You will see how each of the three ingredients of the grammar of graphics (data, aesthetics, geometry) becomes a piece of code, and how the same dataset can be displayed in radically different and informative ways.
For now, the principles in this chapter are the things to keep in mind. Good plots are not the result of decorative talent; they are the result of a small number of decisions made carefully.

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.8 Check your understanding
1. What is the lesson of Anscombe’s quartet?

 It demonstrates that summary statistics are always more reliable than plots. It demonstrates that very different datasets can share nearly identical summary statistics, and that plotting the data is necessary to see what is actually there. It demonstrates that the standard deviation is a misleading statistic. It demonstrates that correlations are unrelated to scatterplots.

2. According to the grammar of graphics, what are the three ingredients of any plot?

 Color, font, and background. Data, aesthetics (mappings from variables to visual channels), and geometry (the visual shape used to represent observations). Title, x-axis label, and y-axis label. The mean, the median, and the standard deviation.

3. Which geometry is most appropriate for showing the distribution of one continuous variable (e.g., the aggression scores of 120 participants)?

 A pie chart. A bar chart of the mean. A histogram or density plot. A scatterplot.

4. Which geometry is most appropriate for showing the relationship between two continuous variables (e.g., weekly playing hours and aggression)?

 A bar chart of the count. A scatterplot. A pie chart. A histogram of one of the variables.

5. Which of the following plots violates the principle “show the data, not just summaries”?

 A boxplot or violin plot per group. A bar chart that shows only the group means, with no individual data points and no indication of spread. A scatterplot with the data points jittered. A histogram of the variable for each group.

6. What is “chart junk”?

 Decorative or non-informative visual elements (excessive gridlines, 3D effects, drop shadows, gradients) that distract from the data. Decorative or non-informative visual elements that do not encode information; they distract the reader and should be removed. Any plot that uses color. Plots that contain too many data points.

7. What is wrong with truncating the y-axis to a narrow range that excludes zero (e.g., showing aggression on a 4.0–6.0 scale when the variable can range from 1 to 10)?

 It compresses the data into too few values. It is the only honest way to show small differences. It visually exaggerates small differences. The bars (or other marks) appear much more different in size than the actual numerical difference would suggest, given the natural range of the variable. It is required by most journals.

8. Why does this chapter recommend avoiding pie charts?

 Pie charts are the best way to compare three or more proportions. Humans compare the heights of bars more accurately than the angles of pie slices, so a bar chart is almost always a better choice than a pie chart for comparing proportions. Pie charts are illegal in scientific publications. Pie charts are equivalent to histograms.

9. How should color be used in a plot?

 It is purely decorative and should be used to make plots more attractive. It should encode information (such as a category or a continuous variable). Use a limited number of distinct colors, prefer colorblind-friendly palettes, and where possible reinforce color with another visual channel such as shape. Color should be avoided in scientific plots; use only black and white. Color should always be assigned in red and green to maximize contrast.

10. What is the recommended order of operations for a typical data-analysis workflow?

 First visualize, then describe, then wrangle. First describe, then visualize, then wrangle. First wrangle (clean, filter, reshape), then describe (compute summaries to sanity-check the wrangling), then visualize (plot what looks important). Wrangling, describing, and visualizing should always be done simultaneously in one operation.

title: 11  Wrangling for psychology research
text:
11.1 Overview
Real research data rarely arrives in the clean, complete state of vgames_study.csv. Participants skip items, demographic categories need to be collapsed, multi-item questionnaires need to be combined into single scale scores, and categorical variables need to be told what order to appear in. This chapter covers the four wrangling skills you will use most often in psychology research:
Each builds directly on the tidyverse tools from Chapter 9. The chapter assumes you have library(tidyverse) loaded.

title: 11  Wrangling for psychology research
text:
handling missing data,
recoding variables with case_when(),
computing composite scores from item-level data,
working with factor variables and reference levels.

title: 11  Wrangling for psychology research
text:
11.2 Missing data
R uses a special value, NA, to represent “missing.” It is not zero, not blank, not a string; it is a marker that the value is unknown. Almost every real dataset has at least some missing values, and how you handle them affects every analysis you do.

11.2.1 Detecting missing values
The function is.na() returns TRUE for each element that is NA and FALSE otherwise:

x <- c(4.2, 3.7, NA, 5.8, NA, 4.1)
is.na(x)
# [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

To count the number of missing values in a vector:

sum(is.na(x))
# [1] 2

sum() counts TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0, so summing the logical vector gives the count of missings. To count missings in every column of a data frame:

sapply(data, function(col) sum(is.na(col)))

This is usually the first thing to run on a fresh dataset. Knowing where the missings are tells you what you can and cannot analyze.


11.2.2 Computing with missing values
Most summary functions return NA when any input is missing, unless you tell them otherwise:

mean(x)                 # NA
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)   # 4.45

na.rm = TRUE tells the function to remove missing values before computing. You will type this argument constantly. This was first introduced in Chapter 6.


11.2.3 Removing rows with missing values
Two common options:

# Keep only rows where every value is non-missing
complete_data <- data |> filter(complete.cases(data))

# Same idea, base R shorthand
complete_data <- na.omit(data)

Both produce a data frame with only complete observations. This is called listwise deletion. It is the simplest approach and is sometimes appropriate, but it can lose a large fraction of your sample if missing values are scattered across many variables. Inspect how much you would lose before applying it:

nrow(data)                            # original sample size
sum(complete.cases(data))             # how many would survive listwise deletion



11.2.4 Filling in missing values
For some variables, replacing missing values with a specific value is reasonable (for example, replacing missing free-text responses with "none"). tidyr::replace_na() does this:

data <- data |>
  mutate(comments = replace_na(comments, "none"))

Replacing numeric missings with the mean of the variable (mean imputation) is sometimes done but is statistically dubious; it shrinks variance and can bias correlations. For serious work, look up multiple imputation in a later course or the mice package.


11.2.5 Why this matters for your sample
The dataset you analyze is not always the dataset you collected. Below is a simple visualization of what happens when you apply listwise deletion to a hypothetical version of our data with some missing aggression scores: the sample shrinks, and (often) the participants who remain differ in subtle ways from those who were dropped.









The number always goes down when you delete. The question is by how much, and whether what is left is still representative.

title: 11  Wrangling for psychology research
text:
11.3 Recoding with case_when()
The dplyr function case_when() is the general-purpose tool for “if this, then that; else if something else, then something else; else…” It is much more readable than nested ifelse() calls and accommodates any number of conditions.
The general form is a list of condition ~ value pairs:

data <- data |>
  mutate(age_band = case_when(
    age < 21          ~ "young",
    age >= 21 & age < 23 ~ "middle",
    age >= 23         ~ "older"
  ))

R checks each row against the conditions in order. The first condition that matches wins. The result is a new variable age_band with one of three values for each participant.
case_when() is used constantly for:

Collapsing categories. For example, combining several gender labels into a smaller set if cell sizes are small:


data <- data |>
  mutate(gender_collapsed = case_when(
    gender == "man"   ~ "man",
    gender == "woman" ~ "woman",
    TRUE              ~ "other"
  ))

The last condition TRUE is a catch-all: any row that did not match a previous condition gets the value "other". (TRUE is always true, so it always matches.)

Binning continuous variables. Creating a high/low split, or quartiles, or theoretically meaningful groups:


data <- data |>
  mutate(hostility_group = case_when(
    trait_hostility <= 3  ~ "low",
    trait_hostility <= 5  ~ "medium",
    trait_hostility > 5   ~ "high"
  ))

A short visualization of the recoded variable confirms the counts:









A binary variable is a special case of the same pattern: two conditions, two values.
A general piece of advice. When you recode, keep both the original variable and the recoded one (use mutate() to add the new variable, not to overwrite the old). Your original measurement is what should appear in your data archive. Recoded variables are derived; if you change your mind about the recoding rules, you want to be able to start over from the original.

title: 11  Wrangling for psychology research
text:
11.4 Computing composite scores
This is the most common wrangling task in psychology that the basic dplyr verbs do not address directly. A questionnaire study typically measures one construct (anxiety, openness, hostility, attitudes toward something) with several items. The analysis treats the construct as a single score per participant. Computing that single score from the individual items, correctly, is the centerpiece of this section.
The procedure has three steps:

Inspect the items. Each row is one participant. Each item is one column.
Reverse-score negatively-worded items. Some items are worded so that agreement indicates less of the construct (e.g., for a hostility scale: “I rarely lose my temper” should be reverse-scored, because high agreement means low hostility). Reversing is a single arithmetic step.
Aggregate. Compute the participant’s mean (or sum) across the now-consistently-coded items.

We illustrate with a small synthetic dataset of five hostility items. (The vgames_study.csv file contains the already-aggregated trait_hostility variable, not the individual items, so we generate items here so you can see the procedure.)

# Five items on a 1-7 scale. h4 is negatively worded.
set.seed(42)
hostility <- data.frame(
  participant_id = 1:120,
  h1 = sample(1:7, 120, replace = TRUE),
  h2 = sample(1:7, 120, replace = TRUE),
  h3 = sample(1:7, 120, replace = TRUE),
  h4 = sample(1:7, 120, replace = TRUE),
  h5 = sample(1:7, 120, replace = TRUE)
)

head(hostility)


11.4.1 Reverse-scoring an item
A 1-7 scale reverses with the formula 8 - x: a 1 becomes a 7, a 4 stays a 4, a 7 becomes a 1. More generally, for a scale from low to high, the reversed value of x is (low + high) - x. On a 1-5 scale that is 6 - x. On a 0-10 scale that is 10 - x.
To reverse-score item 4:

hostility <- hostility |>
  mutate(h4_rev = 8 - h4)

Note that we kept h4 and added h4_rev as a new variable. Do not overwrite the original; you want a clear audit trail of which items were reversed.


11.4.2 Computing the composite
Now that all five items code “high = more hostility,” the composite is the participant’s mean across the five items. The most readable form is explicit:

hostility <- hostility |>
  mutate(hostility_score = (h1 + h2 + h3 + h4_rev + h5) / 5)

For five items this is fine. With twenty items it becomes tedious, and rowMeans() is shorter:

hostility <- hostility |>
  mutate(hostility_score = rowMeans(
    cbind(h1, h2, h3, h4_rev, h5),
    na.rm = TRUE
  ))

rowMeans() takes a matrix or data-frame-like collection of columns and returns the row-wise mean. na.rm = TRUE makes it ignore missing items; without it, a participant who skipped one item would get an NA score. Most psychometric guidance recommends computing the mean only if the participant answered at least some minimum number of items (often two-thirds); flagging participants below that threshold is a separate step that we will not cover here.


11.4.3 Inspecting the result
The composite is a numeric variable on the same scale as the items. To check it, you would look at its distribution.









A composite score also lets you ask whether the construct is related to anything else. For example, is hostility related to aggression? A scatterplot answers that question directly.









(The plot uses the already-aggregated trait_hostility from vgames_study.csv. In your own analyses, the composite you computed and the scatterplot you draw on top of it follow exactly the same pattern.)
The scatterplot uses the visualization principles from Chapter 10: each participant is a single point, color encodes condition (with a colorblind-safe palette), axes are labeled in plain language, and the relationship between the two variables is visible at a glance.

title: 11  Wrangling for psychology research
text:
11.5 Factor variables and reference levels
Categorical variables in R come in two flavors. A character vector is plain text. A factor vector is text plus an explicit list of allowed levels in a specific order. The distinction matters for analysis and for plotting.

11.5.1 Why factors
Most modeling functions in R (regression, ANOVA, t-test, mixed models) need a categorical predictor to be a factor. They use the factor’s first level as the reference category against which other levels are compared. By default, R sorts character vectors alphabetically when it converts them to factors:

factor(c("man", "woman", "non-binary"))
# Levels: man non-binary woman

Alphabetical order is rarely what you want. For an experiment with a control and treatment condition, you almost certainly want control as the reference; alphabetically, control happens to come first, so you are lucky. For our vgames_study data, neutral and violent are also alphabetical, so we are lucky again. For man, non-binary, and woman, alphabetical puts man first, which is the default reference for any model that uses gender. Maybe that is what you want; maybe it is not. You should always set it explicitly.


11.5.2 Setting and changing reference levels
The forcats package (part of the tidyverse) makes factor manipulation readable. The most common operations:
fct_relevel() changes the order of levels. The level you put first becomes the reference:

data <- data |>
  mutate(gender = fct_relevel(gender, "woman", "man", "non-binary"))

After this, woman is the reference category. Models will compare man and non-binary to woman.
fct_recode() renames levels:

data <- data |>
  mutate(condition = fct_recode(condition,
    "Violent game" = "violent",
    "Neutral game" = "neutral"
  ))

This is useful for cleaning labels that arrived in inconsistent or unfriendly forms.
fct_lump() combines rare levels into “Other”:

data <- data |>
  mutate(gender_lumped = fct_lump(gender, n = 2))

n = 2 keeps the two most frequent levels and lumps the rest into Other. Useful when one of your categories has very few participants and your analysis would be unstable if you treated it as its own group.


11.5.3 Why factor order matters for plots
The order of factor levels controls the order in which categories appear on a plot. A plot of gender counts respects alphabetical order by default, which may not be the order you want to communicate.
Default (alphabetical) order:









Custom order (by frequency):









The data are identical. The second plot is easier to read because the bars are in a meaningful order (most frequent to least). fct_infreq() reorders a factor by descending frequency; fct_inorder() keeps the order in which levels first appear in the data; fct_relevel() lets you specify the order explicitly. Picking the right order is a small choice that consistently improves readability.
The same logic applies to models: reordering factor levels does not change the underlying data, but it changes which comparisons appear in the model output and which level is the reference. Setting factor order deliberately is part of preparing data for analysis, not just a cosmetic step for plots.

title: 11  Wrangling for psychology research
text:
11.6 Check your understanding
1. What does NA mean in R?

 A vector of zeros (0). An empty character string (""). A special value, NA, that marks the value as unknown. It is not zero and not blank. It silently removes the corresponding row from the dataset.

2. What does mean(x) return when x is a numeric vector containing one or more NA values, by default?

 NA. Most summary functions return NA when any input is missing, unless you set na.rm = TRUE. The mean of the non-missing values, automatically. An error message and execution stops. The number of missing values.

3. What is “listwise deletion” (also known as keeping only complete cases) likely to do to your dataset?

 It produces a sample identical in size and composition to the original. It produces a smaller sample (only rows with no missing values across the variables used) and the participants who remain can differ systematically from those who were dropped. It fills in missing values with the mean of each column. It silently replaces NA with zero.

4. What is case_when() used for?

 case_when() only works on numeric variables. case_when() is the same as mean() for two groups. case_when() is a readable way to write multiple condition-result pairs; each row gets the value from the first matching condition. It replaces nested ifelse() calls. case_when() always produces a logical vector.

5. When you create a recoded version of a variable, what is the recommended practice?

 Modifying the original variable in place because the new value is intended to overwrite it. Adding the recoded variable as a new column with mutate() and keeping the original. The original is the raw measurement; the recoded variable is derived from it. Renaming the original variable so it cannot be retrieved. Deleting the original variable to save memory.

6. What is the formula to reverse-score an item that was answered on a 1-to-7 scale?

 The reverse of x on a 1-7 scale is 7 - x. The reverse of x on a 1-7 scale is 8 - x. On a 1-5 scale it would be 6 - x. The formula is (low + high) - x. Reverse-scoring is unnecessary if the items are designed correctly. Reverse-scoring uses the rev() function applied to the column.

7. What does rowMeans() do when applied to several columns of a data frame?

 It computes the sum of the items. It assumes there are no missing values; if any item is missing, it errors out. It computes the mean across the named columns row by row. With na.rm = TRUE, missing items are ignored before averaging. It only works on character columns.

8. Why does the order of levels in a factor variable matter for analysis?

 Models in R do not accept factors; they need character vectors. Most modeling functions use the first level of a factor as the reference category against which other levels are compared. R sorts levels alphabetically by default, which is often not the reference you intended. Factors automatically reverse-score themselves. Factors are a synonym for numeric vectors.

9. What does fct_relevel(gender, "woman", "man", "non-binary") do?

 It renames the levels of a factor. It removes the factor entirely. It reorders the levels of a factor; the level you place first becomes the reference category. It deletes rows that contain a specific level.

10. Two bar charts of the same gender variable look different because one shows the bars in alphabetical order and the other in descending frequency. What is the relationship between the two plots?

 The data have changed; the second plot shows a different dataset. The data are identical. Only the order of the factor levels has changed, which controls the order of the bars on the x-axis. The second plot is wrong because it does not show the categories alphabetically. The second plot uses a different geom than the first.

title: 12  Advanced wrangling (optional)
text:
12.1 Overview
This chapter is optional. The wrangling skills covered in Chapters 8, 9, and 11 are sufficient for most analyses in a typical psychology study. The four topics here come up in specific situations rather than universally, and you can skip the chapter on a first reading and come back when one of these situations actually arises.
The topics are:
Each is presented briefly with a single concrete example. If you need to do one of these tasks seriously, the section here is a starting point; the relevant package’s documentation will go further.

title: 12  Advanced wrangling (optional)
text:
Joining datasets when you have data spread across multiple files.
Standardizing and centering numeric variables, which you will need before many analyses.
String manipulation for cleaning text data that arrived in inconsistent forms.
Detecting and handling outliers.

title: 12  Advanced wrangling (optional)
text:
12.2 Joining datasets
Research data often arrives in pieces. You might have one file with participant demographics, another with trial-by-trial responses from the experiment, another with self-report questionnaires administered later. Before analysis, these need to be combined into a single data frame, one row per (participant or trial).
The dplyr family of join functions handles this. Each takes two data frames, x and y, plus a by argument that names the column they have in common (the key). The functions differ in what they do with rows that have no match on the other side.
The four join functions you will use most often:

left_join(x, y, by = "key") keeps all rows of x, and for each row brings in the matching columns from y. If a row in x has no match in y, the new columns are filled with NA. This is the most common case: keep your main dataset complete, add information from elsewhere where you can.
inner_join(x, y, by = "key") keeps only rows that have a match in both x and y.
full_join(x, y, by = "key") keeps every row from both sides, with NA where the match is missing on either side.
anti_join(x, y, by = "key") keeps rows of x that do not have a match in y. Useful for finding what is missing.

A small concrete example. Suppose alongside vgames_study.csv you also have a short questionnaire administered one week later, in a separate file with one row per participant and a wellbeing score. The two data frames share the column participant_id.

# Read the two files
data <- read.csv("data/vgames_study.csv")
followup <- read.csv("data/wellbeing_followup.csv")

# Combine: keep all participants from the main dataset, add wellbeing where available
combined <- data |> left_join(followup, by = "participant_id")

After this, combined is a data frame with all 120 participants from data and an additional wellbeing column. Participants who did not complete the follow-up have NA in that column.
A few practical pieces of advice. First, before joining, check that the key column has the same type in both data frames (integer vs character are not equivalent for matching). Second, check for duplicate keys; if data has one row per participant but followup has two rows for the same participant, the join will produce two rows in the result, which is usually a bug. The functions duplicated() and table(data$participant_id) are useful sanity checks. Third, after joining, run nrow() and sum(is.na(new_column)) to confirm the result has the expected shape.

title: 12  Advanced wrangling (optional)
text:
12.3 Standardizing and centering
Many analyses require numeric variables to be standardized (rescaled to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1) or centered (rescaled to have mean 0, without changing the standard deviation). Both are routine and both are easy to do, but they are easy to forget if you do not have a workflow for them.

12.3.1 z-scores with scale()
The base R function scale() computes a z-score: subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation. The result has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

data <- data |>
  mutate(aggression_z = as.numeric(scale(aggression)))

scale() returns a one-column matrix by default; wrapping it in as.numeric() turns it into a plain vector, which is what mutate() and downstream functions expect.
z-scores are useful when you want to put variables on a common scale (so a regression coefficient on a z-scored predictor is the change in the outcome per one-standard-deviation change in the predictor), and when you want to identify extreme observations (a z-score above 3 in absolute value is often used as a rough outlier rule, though see the outliers section below).


12.3.2 Mean-centering
For some analyses, especially those involving interactions or moderation, you want to center the variable on its mean without rescaling the variance:

data <- data |>
  mutate(aggression_centered = aggression - mean(aggression))

The centered variable has mean 0 and the same standard deviation as the original. Centering predictors before computing an interaction term reduces the correlation between the interaction term and the main effects, which makes the regression coefficients easier to interpret. This is standard practice in psychology when fitting models with interactions.


12.3.3 Group-mean centering
In multilevel and longitudinal data, you sometimes want to center a variable on its group mean, not the grand mean. For example, in a study where each participant provides multiple observations, you may want to separate within-person variability (deviation from the participant’s own average) from between-person variability (how participants differ from each other on average).
Using the group_by() + mutate() pattern from Chapter 9:

data <- data |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  mutate(aggression_group_centered = aggression - mean(aggression)) |>
  ungroup()

Here we have centered each participant’s aggression score on the mean of their condition. This is a small step at the wrangling level but is the foundation of correctly specified multilevel models. In a course on multilevel modeling you will see this distinction (within-person vs between-person centering) elaborated in much more detail.

title: 12  Advanced wrangling (optional)
text:
12.4 String manipulation
Real text data is messy. The same answer might appear as "Male", "male", "M", " male" (note the leading space), or "male " (trailing space). Before analysis, you usually need to clean these into a consistent form. The stringr package (part of the tidyverse) provides functions for this. All of them take a string vector and return a transformed string vector.
The most commonly useful:

str_to_lower(x) converts to lowercase. Solves most case-inconsistency problems in one step.
str_to_upper(x) the reverse.
str_trim(x) removes leading and trailing whitespace.
str_replace(x, pattern, replacement) replaces the first occurrence of a pattern within each string.
str_replace_all(x, pattern, replacement) replaces all occurrences.
str_detect(x, pattern) returns a logical vector: does each string contain the pattern?
str_sub(x, start, end) extracts a substring (by character position).

A small example. Suppose a free-text gender column arrived in messy form. Clean it like this:

data <- data |>
  mutate(gender = str_trim(gender)) |>          # remove leading/trailing spaces
  mutate(gender = str_to_lower(gender)) |>      # normalize case
  mutate(gender = case_when(                    # collapse variants
    gender %in% c("m", "male", "man")     ~ "man",
    gender %in% c("f", "female", "woman") ~ "woman",
    gender %in% c("nb", "non-binary", "nonbinary") ~ "non-binary",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))

Notice that the case-collapse step in the middle uses case_when() from Chapter 11. String functions get the data into a consistent form; case_when() then maps the cleaned strings to a final, controlled set of categories.
For more sophisticated patterns, stringr also supports regular expressions (a notation for describing patterns in text). Regular expressions are powerful but have their own learning curve; the stringr cheatsheet on the tidyverse website is the best starting point if you find yourself needing them.

title: 12  Advanced wrangling (optional)
text:
12.5 Detecting and handling outliers
An outlier is an observation that is unusually extreme relative to the rest of the data. Outliers matter because many statistical methods are sensitive to them: a single very extreme point can change the slope of a regression line, the value of a mean, or the result of a t-test. Identifying outliers and deciding what to do about them is a separate analytic step that you should think through deliberately, not on autopilot.

12.5.1 Detecting outliers with z-scores
A common rule of thumb: an observation with a z-score greater than 3 (or less than -3) in absolute value is considered a potential outlier. After computing the z-score, you can flag such observations:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    aggression_z = as.numeric(scale(aggression)),
    is_outlier_z = abs(aggression_z) > 3
  )

# How many?
sum(data$is_outlier_z)

This rule is simple and easy to communicate, but it has known weaknesses. It assumes the distribution is roughly normal; if the underlying distribution is skewed or has natural heavy tails, the rule will flag too many observations (or too few). It is also influenced by the outliers themselves: extreme values inflate the standard deviation, which can mask other outliers.


12.5.2 Detecting outliers with the IQR rule
A more robust rule uses the interquartile range (IQR), the distance between the 25th and 75th percentiles:

q1 <- quantile(data$aggression, 0.25)
q3 <- quantile(data$aggression, 0.75)
iqr <- q3 - q1

data <- data |>
  mutate(is_outlier_iqr = aggression < (q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | aggression > (q3 + 1.5 * iqr))

sum(data$is_outlier_iqr)

Observations more than 1.5 IQRs below the 25th percentile or above the 75th percentile are flagged. This is the rule that produces the “whiskers” of a boxplot, and it is more robust than the z-score rule because percentiles are less influenced by extreme values than means and standard deviations.


12.5.3 Deciding what to do
Detecting an outlier is the easy part. Deciding what to do about it requires judgment. The options:

Keep all observations and report. The most defensible choice in many cases. Real data has outliers; pretending they do not exist can produce misleading inferences. Report the values, run the analysis with and without them, and discuss any difference.
Trim (remove). Drop the outliers and re-run the analysis. This is sometimes appropriate when you have strong reason to believe the value is an error (e.g., a reaction time of -50 milliseconds, or a score of 99 on a 1-7 scale). Always report what was trimmed and why.
Winsorize. Replace each extreme value with the nearest non-outlier value (e.g., replace anything above the 95th percentile with the 95th-percentile value). Preserves the participant in the dataset but reduces the influence of the extreme value on the analysis.

The rule that matters across all of these: decisions about outliers should be made and pre-registered before looking at the analysis results, and should be reported transparently. The temptation to drop “inconvenient” observations after seeing how they affect the result is one of the better-documented sources of false-positive findings in the published literature. Pre-specifying your outlier rule (and your rule for what to do with detected outliers) protects you and your reader from that temptation.

title: 12  Advanced wrangling (optional)
text:
12.6 Check your understanding
1. What does left_join(x, y, by = "key") do?

 It keeps all rows of x and brings in matching columns from y, filling NA where there is no match in y. It keeps only rows that appear in both x and y. It deletes rows of x that have no match in y. It keeps every row of both x and y, replacing the data of one with the data of the other.

2. What happens if the key column has duplicate values in one of the two data frames being joined?

 It produces an error. The join produces multiple rows in the result for each duplicated key, which is usually a bug. You should check for duplicates with duplicated() or table() before joining. It silently averages the duplicated values. Duplicated keys are impossible in dplyr joins.

3. What does scale() do to a numeric variable?

 It returns a vector with the same mean and standard deviation as the original. It removes all NA values from the variable. It returns a z-scored version of the variable: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation, so the result has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. It scales the values to lie between 0 and 1.

4. What is the purpose of mean-centering a predictor before fitting a model with interactions or moderation?

 It changes the result of a regression in unpredictable ways. It puts the variable on a scale centered at 0 (mean of the centered variable is zero) without changing its standard deviation; this is useful for fitting interaction or moderation models because it reduces collinearity between main effects and the interaction term. It is the same as z-scoring. It removes outliers from the variable.

5. What does str_to_lower(x) do?

 Reads the file as a UTF-8 string. Converts the string to lowercase, which solves most case-inconsistency problems in one step (e.g., "Male" and "male" both become "male"). Counts how many lowercase letters appear in the string. Sorts the elements of a string vector.

6. What does str_trim(x) do?

 It checks that all strings have the same length. It removes leading and trailing whitespace from each string, so " male " becomes "male". It removes all spaces from the string, including internal ones. It converts the string to a number.

7. What is an outlier?

 An observation that is missing. An observation that is unusually extreme relative to the rest of the data; outliers matter because many statistical methods are sensitive to them. An observation that disagrees with the researcher's hypothesis. An observation collected in a different session.

8. What is a known weakness of the “z-score above 3” rule for detecting outliers?

 It works best on heavily skewed distributions. It is completely insensitive to the distribution of the data. It is sensitive to the distribution (it implicitly assumes roughly normal data) and to the outliers themselves, because extreme values inflate the standard deviation that the rule depends on. It is required by all reputable journals.

9. What does the IQR rule flag as outliers?

 Observations below the 25th percentile minus 1.5 times the interquartile range, or above the 75th percentile plus 1.5 times the IQR, are flagged. These are also the values that fall outside a boxplot's whiskers. Observations more than 1.5 standard deviations from the mean. All observations in the bottom or top 25 percent of the distribution. Observations that are exactly equal to the median.

10. What is the recommended approach to handling detected outliers?

 Always drop them, because they are by definition errors. Always keep them and never discuss them. Make the decision (keep, trim, or winsorize) deliberately, ideally before looking at the analysis results, and report transparently what was done and why. Running the analysis with and without the flagged observations and comparing is good practice. Replace them with the median of the variable.

title: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model
text:
13.1 Where we are now
Section 1 taught you how R works. Section 2 taught you how to take a raw data file and turn it into the specific summaries and plots you need to actually look at the data. Together, those two sections covered the work that precedes any analysis.
Section 3 is about analysis itself, and specifically about a single, unifying framework that organizes most of the statistics you will use as a researcher in psychology and the social sciences. That framework is statistical modeling. It is not a single technique; it is a way of thinking that connects descriptive statistics (which you already know) to linear regression, ANOVA, t-tests, multiple regression, and beyond. Once you see the framework, the techniques fall into place as small variations on a single theme.
This chapter is the first of eight chapters on statistical modeling and regression. It is purely conceptual; it has no regression code. The goal is to install three ideas firmly enough that the rest of Section 3 can build on them: what data is, what a model is, and why the mean (which you have computed many times by now) can be thought of as the simplest possible model of a dataset. The next chapter will put those ideas to work with R code.
crumbs: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model

title: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model
text:
13.2 What is data?
You have already worked with data throughout this book, especially in Section 2. We pause here to state explicitly the small set of facts about data that the rest of Section 3 will rely on.

13.2.1 The structure of a dataset
You met this in Chapter 5 and reinforced it in Chapter 8: a dataset is a rectangular table.

Each row is one case, observation, or unit of analysis. In vgames_study.csv, each row is one participant.
Each column is one variable. In vgames_study.csv, the columns are participant_id, age, gender, condition, hours_weekly, trait_hostility, empathy, and aggression.

This is the standard structure that statistical procedures expect. Almost all of the techniques in the rest of this book assume your data is organized this way (sometimes called tidy data, in the tidyverse sense). When raw data does not look like this, the work of Chapters 8 through 12 turns it into something that does.


13.2.2 The type of each variable matters
The kind of variable a column contains determines what you can do with it. The three types you will see most often in psychology:
Continuous variables (also called numeric or quantitative) take values on a numeric scale. The differences between values are meaningful. In our dataset: age (in years), hours_weekly (hours per week), trait_hostility (1 to 7), empathy (1 to 7), aggression (1 to 10). You can compute means, standard deviations, and correlations on continuous variables.
Categorical variables (also called nominal or qualitative) take values that represent groups or categories, with no natural numeric scale. In our dataset: condition ("violent" or "neutral"), gender ("man", "woman", "non-binary"). The “mean” of these values is meaningless: there is no average of "violent" and "neutral". What you compute on categorical variables are counts and proportions.
Ordinal variables take values that have a natural order but where the differences between values are not necessarily equal. A common example is education level (high school, bachelor’s, master’s, doctorate): there is an order, but the gap between “high school” and “bachelor’s” is not necessarily the same as the gap between “master’s” and “doctorate.” For this book, we treat ordinal variables simply, often analyzing them as if they were continuous when there are enough categories to support that.
A useful preview of why this matters: in the regression models you will fit in the rest of Section 3, R needs to know which kind of variable each predictor is. Treating a categorical variable as if it were continuous, or vice versa, produces wrong answers. We will see in Chapter 17 how R handles categorical predictors automatically, using the factor variables you met in Chapter 11.


















The two pictures above use the same dataset but answer different questions. For the categorical variable condition, we ask “how many participants are in each category?” and the answer is a count per bar. For the continuous variable aggression, we ask “what is the shape of the distribution?” and the answer is a histogram. The natural summary in the first case is a count; the natural summary in the second is something like a mean, accompanied by a measure of spread.
crumbs: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model

title: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model
text:
13.3 What is a model?
Statistics borrows the word model from everyday life, where it means roughly the same thing.
A map is a model of a territory. The map of the Vienna U-Bahn does not show every building, every park, every cobblestone. It shows only the train lines and stops. The map is “wrong” in a strict sense, in that it omits almost everything in the city. But it is useful for a specific purpose: getting around the subway. A map that showed every brick in every building would not be useful at all; it would be as complex as the city itself.
A caricature is a model of a face. It exaggerates a few features (a prominent chin, a large pair of eyebrows) and ignores the rest. It captures something essential about the person while leaving out detail.
A weather forecast is a model of the atmosphere. It compresses the enormously complex dynamics of pressure, temperature, humidity, wind, terrain, and ocean temperatures into “tomorrow will be 18 degrees and partly cloudy.” It is not a complete description of what the air will do tomorrow; it is a useful summary.
All models share two features:

They simplify: they leave things out.
They are useful for specific purposes, but not for everything.

The statistician George Box, who worked on industrial quality control and is widely cited in this context, summarized this with a now-famous sentence:

All models are wrong, but some are useful.

The point is not that “wrong” is a problem to be avoided. The point is that simplification is the whole job of a model. A model that did not simplify would be the data itself, restated in slightly different words. There would be no insight in it.
In statistics, a model is a precise, mathematical, simplified description of the data. Like the map, it leaves things out. Like the map, it is useful for some purposes (predicting, summarizing, comparing groups, testing hypotheses) and not others. And like the map, simpler is sometimes better, even if a more complex model would technically describe the data more accurately.
crumbs: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model

title: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model
section: 13.4 The mean as the simplest model
text:
13.4 The mean as the simplest model
We can now state something you have already used many times in a new way. You have been computing means since Chapter 6 (where mean() was introduced as a summary function). You computed group means in Chapter 8 and again in Chapter 9 (where you also computed residuals from the mean and saw that the sum of squared residuals shrank when you used the group means instead of the grand mean).
Here is the new way to think about all of that work:
The mean is a statistical model. It is the simplest possible model of a dataset. The model says: “if you had to predict any participant’s score on this variable, predict the mean.”
Consider the aggression scores of the 120 participants in vgames_study. The mean is approximately 4.89. We can describe a model that uses this single number:

Model 1: every participant’s predicted aggression score is 4.89.

This model is obviously wrong for most participants: participant 5 scored 6.7, participant 12 scored 5.7, participant 1 scored 4.2. None of them scored exactly 4.89. But the model is also obviously useful: it gives a single, communicable summary of the 120 numbers. If someone asked “about how aggressive were participants in this study?” the answer “around 4.89 on a 1 to 10 scale” is far more useful than handing them all 120 raw scores.









The red vertical line is the model’s single prediction. The grey bars are the 120 observed scores. The distance between each bar and the red line, for each participant, is what the model misses. Those distances will be the topic of the next chapter.

13.4.1 Why this matters
Once you accept that the mean is a model, three things follow.
First, all other statistical techniques are extensions of this idea. In the next chapter we will look at the differences between observed and predicted scores (residuals) and at a way to quantify how badly the model misses (sum of squared residuals). In Chapter 15 we will replace the single mean with a line: a model that predicts a different value for each participant depending on a continuous predictor. In Chapter 17 we will replace the line with a model that uses several predictors at once. In every case, the structure is the same: data, a model that makes a prediction for each observation, residuals (what the model misses), and a measure of how well the model fits.
Second, a more complex model is not automatically better. A model that predicted each participant’s exact score (using 120 numbers, one per participant) would have zero residuals. It would be a “perfect fit.” It would also be useless: it would not simplify anything, it would not reveal any pattern, and it would not generalize to participants you have not yet measured. The art is to choose a model simple enough to be informative and complex enough to capture the patterns you care about. This trade-off has a formal name, the bias-variance trade-off, and it will appear explicitly in Chapter 19.
Third, modeling and inference are different activities. Everything described in this chapter, and in the rest of Section 3 up to Chapter 18, is descriptive. We describe data; we fit models; we compare how well they fit. We do not make claims about whether an effect is “statistically significant,” whether the slope in a population is different from zero, or whether the result generalizes to people we did not sample. Those are questions of statistical inference, a separate set of ideas that will appear in a later section of the book. Keeping description and inference separate in your mind is, in our view, one of the most useful intellectual habits in statistics.
crumbs: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model

title: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model
text:
13.5 Looking ahead
Chapter 14 takes the same ideas and makes them concrete in R. You will compute residuals from the grand mean and from group means on a small dataset; you will compute the sum of squared residuals for each; and you will see that the group-means model has a smaller sum of squared residuals, exactly as you did with the aggression data in Chapter 9. This time the framing is different: you are not just computing a sum, you are evaluating the fit of a model.
Then Chapter 15 introduces the simple linear model, which replaces the one-number-per-group structure with a continuous predictor and a line. By the end of Chapter 16 you will be fitting and interpreting your first regression models in R.

title: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model
text:
13.6 Further reading
Danielle Navarro’s free textbook Learning Statistics with R (version 0.6) is an excellent companion reference. Chapter 5 (“Descriptive statistics”) covers central tendency and variability from a more traditional descriptive-statistics perspective, and Chapter 2 (“A brief introduction to research design,” especially Section 2.2 on scales of measurement) goes deeper into variable types. The book is available at https://learningstatisticswithr.com.
crumbs: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model

title: 13  Data and the idea of a statistical model
text:
13.7 Check your understanding
1. What is a “dataset” in the form most statistical procedures expect?

 A folder containing the script and the data files for an analysis. A rectangular table in which each row is one observation (one case, e.g., one participant) and each column is one variable. This is sometimes called “tidy” data. A single number summarizing many observations. Any file in the project, regardless of its structure.

2. Why does the type of a variable (continuous, categorical, ordinal) matter?

 It is purely cosmetic; the type of a variable does not affect what you can do with it in R. The type determines which operations and summaries make sense. The mean of a continuous variable is meaningful; the “mean” of a categorical variable is not, and R's statistical procedures treat categorical and continuous variables differently. Only continuous variables can be analyzed in R. Categorical variables and continuous variables are treated identically.

3. What is a statistical model?

 It is a perfect, exact description of the data. It is a single number summarizing the data. A simplified, useful representation of something complex. Models leave things out; the simplification is the point. “All models are wrong, but some are useful.” It is the dataset itself, viewed in a different form.

4. What is the meaning of George Box’s statement “All models are wrong, but some are useful”?

 It means a good model is one that perfectly reproduces every data point. It captures the idea that all models simplify, and therefore are imperfect descriptions of reality, but a well-chosen model is still useful for a specific purpose. It means statistics is unreliable. It means we should avoid using models when possible.

5. In what sense is the mean of a dataset a statistical model?

 It is too simple to be considered a model. It is a model: it makes a single prediction (the mean value) for every observation, simplifying the dataset into one number. Subsequent chapters build on this idea by introducing more elaborate models that make different predictions for different observations. It is the same as a regression. It is too complex to be useful as a model.

6. What is the trade-off between simple and complex models?

 The model is automatically better as it gets more complex. There is no trade-off; simplicity is always better. A more complex model can fit the observed data more closely (smaller residuals) but tends to capture noise as well as signal; an overly simple model misses real patterns. The art is choosing a model simple enough to be informative and complex enough to capture the patterns of interest. Complex models are easier to interpret than simple ones.

7. What is the difference between modeling and inference, as introduced in this chapter?

 Inference is a more advanced form of modeling that always uses the same equations. Modeling means describing a dataset with a simplified representation (and is the topic of Section 3). Inference is the separate set of activities concerned with making claims about populations or testing hypotheses from sample data. Keeping the two activities mentally separate is a useful habit. Modeling and inference are synonyms. Modeling uses sample data; inference uses population data.

title: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models
text:
14.1 Overview
Chapter 13 introduced the idea that the mean of a dataset can be thought of as the simplest possible statistical model: it makes one prediction (the mean value) for every observation. This chapter takes that idea and turns it into something you can compute in R. By the end of the chapter you will have:
This is the same logic you applied to the aggression scores at the end of Chapter 9 (where you compared SS_grand to SS_group on the vgames_study dataset). The new thing here is the framing: each calculation is the fit of a specific model, and choosing between models is a comparison of how well each fits.
crumbs: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models

title: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models
text:
computed the residuals of two competing models on a small dataset,
quantified each model’s overall miss with the sum of squared residuals,
shown that a model that makes a separate prediction for each experimental condition fits better than a model that makes one prediction for everyone.
crumbs: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models

title: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models
text:
14.2 Residuals: what the model misses
For any model that makes a prediction for each observation, the residual of an observation is the simple difference
\[
\text{residual} = \text{observed} - \text{predicted}.
\]
If a participant scored 6 on a 1-10 scale and the model predicted 5, the residual is +1: the participant scored one point above what the model expected. If a participant scored 3 and the model predicted 5, the residual is -2: the participant scored two points below the model’s prediction. The residual is positive when the model under-predicts, negative when it over-predicts, and zero when the model is exactly right.
Residuals are the central diagnostic quantity in statistical modeling. The sizes of the residuals tell you how well the model fits; the patterns in the residuals (across rows, across groups, across time) tell you whether the model is missing something systematic.
For the mean-only model from Chapter 13, every prediction is the same value (the mean). So every residual is just the observation’s distance from the mean.
crumbs: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models

title: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models
text:
14.3 A small worked example
The rest of this chapter uses a small fictional dataset inspired by a classic social-psychology paradigm called Cyberball, developed by Williams and colleagues to study social ostracism. In the paradigm, participants play a simple virtual ball-tossing game on a computer with two other “players” who they believe are also participants, but who are actually controlled by the experimenter.



Schematic illustration of a three-player Cyberball game. The participant is one of the three figures; the other two appear to be other players but are in fact controlled by the experimenter, who decides whether and how often the ball is thrown to the participant.


There are two experimental conditions. In the inclusion condition, the ball is shared among all three players roughly evenly: the participant receives the ball regularly throughout the game and is, in effect, a full member of the group. In the exclusion condition, the two confederate “players” stop throwing the ball to the participant after a few initial passes, and continue tossing only between themselves for the remainder of the game; the participant is socially excluded from the group activity. After the game, participants complete self-report measures, here a 1-7 self-esteem scale. The question is whether being excluded lowers self-esteem.
We construct the dataset by hand so that you can verify every calculation that follows. Type these lines into your R script:

library(tidyverse)

cyberball <- data.frame(
  participant = 1:8,
  condition   = c("Exclusion", "Exclusion", "Exclusion", "Exclusion",
                  "Inclusion", "Inclusion", "Inclusion", "Inclusion"),
  self_esteem = c(2.5, 3.0, 4.0, 2.5,
                  5.5, 4.5, 6.0, 5.0)
)

cyberball

Eight participants, four per condition, one self-esteem score per participant. We will fit two competing models to these scores and compare how well each one fits.
crumbs: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models

title: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models
text:
14.4 Model 1: the grand-mean model
The simplest model says: ignore which condition each participant was in; predict the grand mean of self_esteem for everyone.
Compute the grand mean and store it. Then use mutate() (from Chapter 9) to add a column with the model’s prediction and a column with the residual:

grand_mean <- mean(cyberball$self_esteem)
grand_mean
# returns 4.125

cyberball <- cyberball |>
  mutate(predicted_grand = grand_mean,
         residual_grand  = self_esteem - predicted_grand)

cyberball

The residuals sum to zero. This is always true of residuals from the mean: the mean is the value at which positive and negative deviations exactly cancel.

sum(cyberball$residual_grand)

The residuals are not small. Some participants are more than 1.5 points away from the grand-mean prediction. Visually:









Each grey segment shows how far one participant’s actual score is from the model’s single prediction (the red line). The grey segments are the residuals. Visually, they are substantial, especially for the inclusion participants who all sit well above the grand mean and for several exclusion participants who sit well below.

title: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models
section: 14.5 Why we cannot just sum the residuals: squaring
text:
14.5 Why we cannot just sum the residuals: squaring
We need a single number that quantifies how well the model fits, and the residuals are the obvious building blocks. But, as just noted, the residuals always sum to zero. The positive and negative deviations cancel out, and the sum tells you nothing about the size of the errors.
The standard fix is to square each residual before summing:
\[
\text{SS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\text{observed}_i - \text{predicted}_i)^2.
\]
This is the sum of squared residuals (or sum of squared errors), often abbreviated SS. You met it in Chapter 9 when you computed SS_grand and SS_group on the aggression data.
Two reasons squaring is the standard choice:

Squaring removes the sign. Negative and positive residuals both contribute positively to the sum, so the cancellation problem disappears.
Squaring penalizes large residuals more than small ones. A residual of 2 contributes 4 to the SS; a residual of 1 contributes only 1. Being off by a lot is treated as much worse than being off by a little. For most modeling problems in psychology this matches the kind of error you want to minimize.

In R, on the residuals we already computed:

SS_grand <- sum(cyberball$residual_grand^2)
SS_grand
# returns 12.875

The number 12.875 is the total squared error of the grand-mean model on these eight observations. It has no natural interpretation in isolation; it is the comparison to the SS of another model that gives it meaning.
crumbs: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models

title: 14  The mean as a model: residuals, fit, and comparing models
text:
14.6 Model 2: the group-means model
A slightly less naive model uses two predictions instead of one: predict the mean of the exclusion condition for exclusion participants, and the mean of the inclusion condition for inclusion participants. The model is more complex (two numbers instead of one), and it uses information the previous model ignored (which condition each participant was in).
Using the group_by() + mutate() + ungroup() pattern from Chapter 9 (the same pattern you used to add a per-group statistic as a column):

cyberball <- cyberball |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  mutate(predicted_group = mean(self_esteem)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(residual_group = self_esteem - predicted_group)

cyberball

The exclusion group’s mean is 3.00 and the inclusion group’s mean is 5.25, so predicted_group is 3.00 for the first four rows and 5.25 for the last four. The residuals are each participant’s distance from their own condition mean.
