title: 25  Two roles, multiple testing, and pre-registration
text:
25.11 Check your understanding
1. What is the distinction between the analyst role and the claim-maker role?

 The analyst commits to one pre-specified hypothesis; the claim-maker explores the dataset without restriction. The analyst and the claim-maker are different people, since the same person cannot legitimately play both roles in a single project. The analyst always reports calibrated p-values; the claim-maker reports only effect sizes and confidence intervals without any p-value at all. The analyst explores the data and generates hypotheses without making formal claims; the claim-maker pre-specifies the procedure and offers calibrated inferences to be acted upon by readers.

2. Why does the Neyman-Pearson framework require a procedure that is fixed independently of the data?

 Because data-dependent procedures use the same reference distribution as fixed procedures, the family-wise alpha is automatically controlled when many tests are run on the same dataset by the researcher. Because the Neyman-Pearson decision rule says reject if p < alpha; once that rule is in place, no further specification of the procedure is needed for the calibration of the test to hold. Because pre-specifying the procedure is a moral requirement for honest science; the actual statistical calibration of p-values does not depend on whether the procedure was fixed in advance. Because the long-run false-positive rate of the procedure is only equal to alpha when the procedure is fixed independently of the data; data-dependent procedures have a higher actual false-positive rate, often much higher.

3. If you run 5 independent tests, each at α = .05, on data where all five nulls are true, what is the probability of at least one false positive?

 About 64%, because each test has its own independent false-positive rate that adds to the family-wise total. About 23%, because 1 - (1 - .05)^5 ≈ .23; the family-wise rate is the probability of at least one false positive across the five tests. About 5%, because each test is run at alpha = .05 and the rate per test is preserved across the family of tests being performed. About 50%, because the family-wise rate doubles for each additional test added to the analysis under independent testing assumptions.

4. What is the difference between the Bonferroni and Holm corrections?

 Bonferroni compares each p-value to alpha divided by the number of tests; Holm uses the same comparison for the smallest p-value but relaxes the threshold for subsequent ones (alpha / (k - j + 1)); both control the family-wise alpha, but Holm has slightly more power. Bonferroni and Holm both control the false discovery rate by sorting p-values from smallest to largest and comparing each to a different scaled threshold; the choice depends on whether the researcher prefers a one-tailed or two-tailed interpretation of the test. Bonferroni multiplies the observed p-value by the number of tests and reports the adjusted result; Holm does the same but with a square-root transformation to preserve the original alpha level across all the tests. Bonferroni controls the family-wise alpha at the level specified by the researcher; Holm controls the false discovery rate at the same level by using the Benjamini-Hochberg sequential procedure for comparison.

5. What does the Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR) correction control, and when is it appropriate?

 Benjamini-Hochberg controls the family-wise error rate at a stricter level than Bonferroni and Holm, making it more appropriate for primary outcomes in clinical trials and other high-stakes decisions. Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate (the expected proportion of false positives among the rejections), which is more permissive than family-wise control and is appropriate when accepting a small proportion of false positives is tolerable. Benjamini-Hochberg adjusts the alpha level only for the smallest p-value in the family of tests; it ignores the other tests and accepts whatever family-wise alpha results from this single-step adjustment. Benjamini-Hochberg requires the tests to be perfectly independent of each other; when tests are correlated (as they often are in regression analyses) the procedure cannot be applied at all to the family of tests.

6. What is the positive predictive value (PPV) of a research field, in Ioannidis’s framework?

 PPV is the probability that a study has correctly rejected the null hypothesis given the observed p-value and the assumed prior probability of the alternative hypothesis being true in the population. PPV is the probability that a finding reported as significant reflects a true effect; it depends on the prior probability of the hypothesis being true, the power of the study, and the alpha level used in the procedure. PPV is the proportion of all studies in a research field that report a statistically significant result at alpha = .05 across both pre-specified and exploratory analyses run on the same dataset by the same researcher. PPV is the long-run rate at which the procedure correctly rejects the null hypothesis when the null is actually false, assuming the standard test assumptions are met by the data.

7. What does pre-registration do, and why is it useful?

 Pre-registration is a moral commitment that researchers make to themselves about the integrity of their analysis; it has no practical effect on the calibration of the p-values they report in the published paper. Pre-registration replaces all post-data analytic decisions with a fully automated procedure that the software runs without any further input from the researcher about exclusion rules or other specifics. Pre-registration is required by all psychology journals as a condition of publication; without it, no paper can be published regardless of the methodological quality of the analyses. Pre-registration is a public, time-stamped document specifying the procedure in advance of seeing the data; it provides the external evidence a reader needs to know whether reported p-values are calibrated, and constrains how findings are labeled rather than what can be reported.

8. What are p-hacking and HARKing?

 P-hacking is running a single pre-specified analysis on a dataset and reporting the result regardless of whether it is statistically significant; HARKing is reporting only the significant secondary outcomes of a pre-registered confirmatory study. P-hacking is trying many analyses on the same data and reporting only the significant one as if it were the only test run; HARKing (Hypothesizing After Results are Known) is writing up a finding as a pre-specified hypothesis when it was actually noticed in the data. P-hacking is computing the wrong p-value due to a typo in the analysis code; HARKing is writing the methods section of a paper after the results section has been finalized and accepted by the journal. P-hacking is using a stricter alpha level than the conventional .05 to ensure a significant result; HARKing is using a more permissive alpha level after the data show a marginally significant pattern.

9. What is the “garden of forking paths” and why does it matter for inference?

 The garden of forking paths applies only to researchers who consciously p-hack; sincere researchers with a single hypothesis are immune from its effects on their false-positive rate across the analysis of the dataset. Even sincere researchers face the problem because the data they collect informs their analytic choices; the set of analyses that could have been run given different data is large, and the actual false-positive rate of the implicit procedure depends on all the branches, not just the one reported. The garden of forking paths is a metaphor for the difficulty of choosing between Bayesian and frequentist approaches to inference; it has no practical implication for the calibration of p-values in either framework. The garden of forking paths applies only to studies that test more than ten different hypotheses on the same dataset; with fewer tests, the family-wise alpha is automatically controlled by the procedure used.

10. What is equivalence testing, and what role does SESOI play in it?

 Equivalence testing is a Bayesian alternative to frequentist hypothesis testing that computes a posterior probability of equivalence given the data; it does not require the researcher to specify a SESOI before running the test on the data. Equivalence testing changes the alpha threshold to a more permissive value (such as .50) so that the null hypothesis is rejected more often, producing claims of equivalence from any non-significant result in the procedure. Equivalence testing replaces the standard hypothesis test with a chi-squared test of independence; it is appropriate when the outcome is categorical and the predictors are continuous or ordinal in nature. Equivalence testing reframes the question as 'is the effect smaller than SESOI?' using two one-sided tests against the SESOI bounds; rejecting both supports a positive claim that the effect is practically equivalent to zero, addressing the asymmetry of standard hypothesis testing.
